title: Trustworthiness Assessment
text:
Introduction
This freely available eBook provides materials for the semester-long Master’s seminar course “Estimating the Credibility of Past Research” that I deliver at the University of Bern’s Institute of Psychology.
Trustworthiness Assessment asks whether the data and findings reported in a study can be believed. It is distinct from the more well-established assessment of Risk of Bias, which asks whether a study’s design and conduct could have distorted its estimate of an effect. A study can have a low Risk of Bias and still report results that are impossible, fabricated, or the product of critical errors. Cochrane calls these problematic studies: any study “where there are serious questions about the trustworthiness of the data or findings, regardless of whether the study has been formally retracted” (Cochrane, n.d.-a). Such problems may result from research misconduct, such as fabrication or falsification, but also from poor research practices or honest errors, and Cochrane’s editorial policies and implementation guidance set out what review authors and editors should do about them (Cochrane, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). If problematic studies are not identified, they can be included in systematic reviews and guidelines and distort their conclusions. Risk-of-bias tools are not designed to detect these problems, so bespoke tools for trustworthiness assessment are needed (Wilkinson et al., 2026).
One such tool, INSPECT-SR (Investigating Problematic Clinical Trials in Systematic Reviews), was developed through a large international expert consensus to provide standardised criteria for assessing the trustworthiness of randomised controlled trials (Wilkinson et al., 2026). It guides a reviewer through up to 21 checks in four domains: post-publication notices; the study’s conduct, governance, and transparency; its text and figures; and the results it reports. The reviewer then judges whether there are no concerns, some concerns, or serious concerns about the trustworthiness of the trial. In October 2025, Cochrane endorsed INSPECT-SR as an optional tool for authors of systematic reviews of randomised controlled trials who wish to assess the trustworthiness of the trials they include (Cochrane, 2025).
Many of the checks that a Trustworthiness Assessment relies on come from Forensic Meta-Science: an emergent subfield of meta-science that develops and applies methods for testing whether the numbers reported in a study are internally consistent and plausible. For example, whether a mean is possible given the sample size, or whether a p-value matches its test statistic. Much of this work has been done by independent researchers who scrutinise the published literature, often called science sleuths. In written testimony to the US House of Representatives in 2026, Kate Travis, the managing editor of Retraction Watch, described how sleuths are coming together to share tools and organise, citing INSPECT-SR as one product of such efforts, and observed that “the field is rapidly professionalizing” (Travis, 2026).
This book is intended as part of that ongoing professionalisation: it sets out the methods of forensic meta-science and trustworthiness assessment, the assumptions they rest on, and how their results should be interpreted. While the INSPECT-SR Guidance website contains the current guidance for the application of its various checks, it is not intended to provide a deep understanding of the methods themselves, or other measures beyond the current scope of INSPECT-SR that are indevelopment or more suited to studies in other areas or using other designs (e.g., psychology articles on non-RCTs). I intend this book to provide that training (see below for links to other resources).
This book is split into five parts:

4.1 Test yourself: (mis)interpretations of p-values
The p-value is the most widely reported inferential statistic in psychology and health research, and it is also among the most widely misunderstood.
Although there is an entirely separate chapter on specific common misinterpretations of p-values later, it is worth beginning this one with an assessment of our own (mis)understandings, before discussing correct interpretations and deeper understandings of the p-value.
Answer all six statements, then click the button at the bottom to see how you did.

title: 4  Understanding p-values ✎ Draft
text:
Suppose you have a treatment that you suspect may alter performance on a certain task. You compare the means of your control and experimental groups (say 20 subjects in each sample). Further, suppose you use a simple independent means t-test and your result is (t = 2.7, df = 18, p = 0.01). Please mark each of the statements below as “true” or “false”. “False” means that the statement does not follow logically from the above premises. Also note that one, several or none of the statements may be correct.

You have absolutely disproved the null hypothesis (that is, there is no difference between the population means). TRUEFALSE
You have found the probability of the null hypothesis being true. TRUEFALSE
You have absolutely proved your experimental hypothesis (that there is a difference between the population means). TRUEFALSE
You can deduce the probability of the experimental hypothesis being true. TRUEFALSE
You know, if you decide to reject the null hypothesis, the probability that you are making the wrong decision. TRUEFALSE
You have a reliable experimental finding in the sense that if, hypothetically, the experiment were repeated a great number of times, you would obtain a significant result on 99% of occasions. TRUEFALSE




Why is each statement true or false?

All six statements are false. Each one corresponds to a recognisable fallacy: the illusion of certainty (statements 1 and 3; Section 4.3.1), the inverse probability fallacy (statements 2, 4, and 5; Section 4.3.2), and the replication delusion (statement 6; Section 4.3.3).

Certainty (disproof). A significance test gives a probabilistic statement about data, not a proof. Data this extreme occur under the null model 1% of the time, so the null hypothesis has not been disproved.
Inverse probability. The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme given the null model, \(P(D \mid H_0)\). It is not the probability of the null hypothesis given the data, \(P(H_0 \mid D)\). Getting from one to the other requires a prior probability for \(H_0\), which a significance test does not use.
Certainty (proof). The mirror image of statement 1. Rejecting the null does not prove the alternative, and even if a difference exists, it does not establish that the experimental hypothesis’s explanation for it is correct.
Inverse probability, again. The probability of the experimental hypothesis is no more deducible from p than the probability of the null is.
Error-rate confusion. This reads p as the probability that rejecting \(H_0\) is a mistake, i.e., \(P(H_0 \mid \text{significant result})\). That is the false discovery risk, which depends on the prior probability of \(H_0\) and on statistical power, neither of which is given. The p-value is also not the Type I error rate: α is fixed before the study and describes the long-run behaviour of the procedure, not the probability of error in this particular decision.
Replication fallacy. 1 − p is not the probability of a significant replication. The replication probability depends on the true effect size and the replication’s power. If the observed effect were exactly the true effect, a same-sized replication would be significant only about 70–75% of the time; and because significant results tend to overestimate effects, the real figure is usually lower.



4.1.1 Prevalence of misinterpretations of p-values
The questionnaire above was first used by Oakes (1986) with academic psychologists, and has since been reused, with minor changes, in Israel (Falk & Greenbaum, 1995), Germany (Haller & Krauss, 2002), Spain (Badenes-Ribera et al., 2015), and China (X.-K. Lyu et al., 2020; Z. Lyu et al., 2018). The wording here follows Haller and Krauss (2002).
If you marked any statement as true, you are in the majority.

Oakes (1986) found that 97% of the 70 academic psychologists he surveyed endorsed at least one of the statements (Gigerenzer, 2018). As summarised by Cohen (1994), 68 of 70 interpreted p as the probability that \(H_0\) is true, and 42 believed a p of .01 implied a 99% chance that a replication would be significant.
Haller and Krauss (2002) gave the questionnaire to students, methodology instructors, and scientists in Germany. As reported by Gigerenzer (2004), none of the 44 psychology students rejected all six statements, compared with 4 of 39 scientists who did not teach statistics and 6 of 30 methodology instructors who did.
Z. Lyu et al. (2018) found that 99% of 362 psychology researchers and students in China endorsed at least one false statement. In a larger sample of 1,479 researchers and students across fields, X.-K. Lyu et al. (2020) found that misinterpretation did not vary meaningfully by degree, field, or career stage, and that respondents were largely unaware of their errors.
Badenes-Ribera et al. (2016) found the inverse-probability fallacy to be the most common error among academic psychologists in Italy and Chile, followed by the replication fallacy.

4.1.1.1 How much should we trust these prevalence estimates?
The direction of this literature is robust, but the precise percentages should be treated with some caution. The questionnaires consist entirely of false statements, which means they cannot distinguish a respondent who misunderstands p-values from one who is uncertain, reads the items charitably, or assumes that at least one statement must be true. McShane and Gal (2017) also note that, as worded, some items can be read as questions about unknown population parameters rather than about the observed result. Similar criticisms have been made of the equivalent questionnaire for confidence intervals (García-Pérez & Alcalá-Quintana, 2016; Miller & Ulrich, 2016). Figures such as “90–99% of researchers endorse at least one false statement” are therefore better read as evidence that misinterpretation is common across fields, career stages, and countries than as well-measured prevalence estimates.



4.1.2 Errors in intro to psych textbooks’ definitions
The errors are not confined to survey responses. They are also in the textbooks.

89%
of introductory psychology textbooks that defined or explained statistical significance did so incorrectly, most often by describing p as the probability that the results occurred by chance (Cassidy et al., 2019).

title: 4  Understanding p-values ✎ Draft
text:
4.2 What a p-value is
It’s important to start by emphasizing that I and this book should not be considered the authoritative source of the definition and interpretation of p-values. For these, see the original sources cited below.

4.2.1 The formal definition
The definition found in most statistics textbooks descends from Fisher’s significance tests and is stated formally by Cox (2006). Choose a test statistic T that measures how far the data depart from what the null hypothesis predicts. The p-value is the probability, calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining a value of T at least as extreme as the one actually observed:
\[
p = P(T \geq t_{\text{obs}};\ H_0)
\]
The semicolon rather than a conditional bar (|) is deliberate. In the frequentist framework \(H_0\) is not a random event with a probability of its own; it is an assumption under which the probability is calculated. Three ingredients are always involved:

A test statistic, such as t, F, or χ², which summarises the data. For a two-sided test, T is the absolute value, e.g., |t|, so that departures in either direction count as extreme.
A reference distribution for that statistic, derived by assuming \(H_0\) is true.
A tail: the probability of the observed value or anything more extreme, not of the observed value alone.

Applied to the quiz scenario: if there were truly no difference between the population means, and the other assumptions of the t-test held, a t statistic at least as far from zero as 2.7 would arise in about 1.5% of repeated studies with 18 degrees of freedom. (The questionnaire’s p = .01 is rounded; the exact two-sided value for t(18) = 2.7 is .015.)
This definition is the key to every statement in the quiz. The p-value is calculated by assuming \(H_0\) is true, so it cannot also be the probability that \(H_0\) is true. As Greenland et al. (2016) put it, it is hard to see how a probability deduced from a set of assumptions could be the probability of those same assumptions.

4.2.1.1 “The model” is the null model
The American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) gives an informal definition that is often quoted:

“the [long-run] probability under a specified statistical model that a statistical summary of the data … would be equal to or more extreme than its observed value.”
American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).

Many readers initially struggle with what “a specified statistical model” refers to. It is not the researcher’s hypothesis, the alternative hypothesis, but rather the null model: the null hypothesis together with every other assumption needed to derive the reference distribution. The statement’s first principle makes this explicit, describing the most common context as “a model, constructed under a set of assumptions, together with a so-called ‘null hypothesis’”. For the independent-samples t-test in the quiz, the null model includes:

The null hypothesis itself: the population means are equal.
Distributional assumptions: the outcome is normally distributed within each group, with equal variances.
Design assumptions: observations are independent, and participants were randomly sampled or randomly assigned.
Analysis and reporting assumptions: the test was planned before seeing the data, and this p-value was not selected for reporting from among many because it was small.

Greenland et al. (2016) build this into their definition.

The p-value is “the [long-run] probability that the chosen test statistic would have been at least as large as its observed value if every model assumption were correct, including the test hypothesis.”
Greenland et al. (2016)

In their terms, \(H_0\) is just the one assumption that has been targeted for testing (the “test hypothesis”); the p-value itself tests all of them at once.



4.2.2 p-values as incompatibility with the null model
It follows that a p-value is best read as a measure of the (in)compatibility between the data and the whole null model. It runs from 0 (the data are completely incompatible with the null model) to 1 (the data are exactly what the null model predicts), so the smaller the p-value, the greater the incompatibility (Greenland et al., 2016).
Lakens (2022) puts the same idea in plainer terms: a p-value tells us how surprising the observed data would be if the null model were true. Surprise depends on what the null model predicts, not only on the size of the observed effect. With a larger sample, the null model predicts mean differences that cluster more tightly around zero, so the same observed difference is more surprising, and its p-value smaller, with 5,000 participants than with 50. Laken’s ebook and online course ‘Improving your Statistical Inferences’ is highly recommended!

A small p-value says that the data would be unusual if every assumption of the null model were true. It does not say which assumption is false. \(H_0\) may be false, or the design may have been compromised, the distributional assumptions may not hold, or the result may have been selected for reporting because it was small.
A large p-value says only that the data are not unusual under the null model. It does not show that \(H_0\) is true: the same data would also be unremarkable under many other hypotheses, and a large p-value can itself result from violated assumptions.

This is why selective reporting matters so much. The ASA statement notes that when many analyses are conducted and only some are reported, the reported p-values become “essentially uninterpretable” (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016). In null-model terms, the assumption that the result was not chosen for its p-value has been violated, so the reference distribution no longer applies.

title: 4  Understanding p-values ✎ Draft
section: 4.3 What many want p-values to be
text:
4.3 What many want p-values to be
Gigerenzer (2018) groups the six false statements in the quiz into three families of wishful thinking: the illusion of certainty (statements 1 and 3), Bayesian wishful thinking, better known as the inverse probability fallacy (statements 2, 4, and 5), and the replication delusion (statement 6). Each reflects something researchers would like a p-value to tell them, but that it cannot.

4.3.1 The illusion of certainty
Statements 1 and 3 treat a significant result as proof: that the null hypothesis has been “absolutely disproved”, or the experimental hypothesis “absolutely proved”. Few researchers would endorse this wording if asked directly, but the underlying intuition shows up whenever a significant result is described as having “shown” or “demonstrated” that an effect exists. The illusion has two parts.
Unusual is not impossible. A small p-value says that the data would be surprising if the null model were true, not that they could not have occurred under it. As Fisher (1935, as cited in Lakens, 2022) put it, the “one chance in a million” will occur with exactly its expected frequency, however surprised we are that it happens to us. This is why \(\alpha\) is a long-run error rate: when the null hypothesis is true, 5% of tests will still be significant at \(\alpha\) = .05, and nothing about any one of those results reveals that it is a false positive. Any single significant result may be one of them, which is why replication matters.
Rejecting the null hypothesis supports “some difference”, not your explanation of it. Even when a significant result correctly indicates that \(H_0\) is false, the statistical alternative it supports (“the population means differ”) is much weaker than the substantive hypothesis the researcher usually has in mind (“the population means differ because of my manipulation, via the mechanism I propose”). Confounds, demand characteristics, measurement artefacts, and many other explanations also predict a difference. A p-value cannot distinguish between them. The gap between what was tested statistically and what is claimed substantively is one of the most common sources of misalignment between an article’s results and its conclusions, and is discussed further in Chapter 16.


4.3.2 The inverse probability fallacy
Statements 2, 4, and 5 come from a mismatch between the question researchers want answered and the question a p-value actually answers.
What most researchers want to know:

Given my data,
how probable is it that my hypothesis is true?

This can be formalised as \(P(H_1 \mid D)\), the probability of the alternative hypothesis given the data. Because the null and alternative hypotheses are mutually exclusive and exhaustive (the effect is either zero or it is not), this is the same question as how probable the null hypothesis is, since \(P(H_1 \mid D) = 1 - P(H_0 \mid D)\).
What a p-value actually tells us:

Given that the null model is true,
how improbable is my data?

This can be formalised as \(P(D \mid H_0)\), the probability of the data given the null hypothesis. Here \(D\) is shorthand for “data at least as extreme as those observed”, and the conditional bar is used loosely for “assuming”, as it usually is in teaching (see the note on the semicolon above).
Significance testing then adds an inferential step that is not part of the probability calculation at all:

Given that the null model is true, how improbable is my data?
If very improbable, we will act as if the alternative hypothesis is true.

This decision rule is what \(\alpha\) controls: in the long run, no more than 5% of tests of true null hypotheses will be significant (given the test’s assumptions and no bias such as uncorrected multiple testing or p-hacking). It does not say how probable any particular hypothesis is.
The p-value, \(P(D \mid H_0)\), and the quantity researchers want, \(P(H_1 \mid D)\), differ in two ways, and misinterpretations usually slip across both at once:

The direction of the conditional is reversed. \(P(D \mid H_0)\) is the probability of the data given the null; \(P(H_0 \mid D)\) is the probability of the null given the data. These can differ enormously. The probability that a person is a smoker given that they have lung cancer is high; the probability that a person has lung cancer given that they smoke is much lower. Treating one as the other is known as the inverse probability fallacy or the transposed conditional. Cohen (1994) made the same point with a syllogism: if a person is an American, they are probably not a member of Congress; this person is a member of Congress; therefore, they are probably not an American. The conclusion is plainly absurd, yet it has the same form as the reasoning behind rejecting \(H_0\) and concluding that \(H_0\) is probably false. A significance test tells us how improbable the data are if \(H_0\) is true, not how improbable \(H_0\) is given the data.
The complement is then taken. Having read p as \(P(H_0 \mid D)\), it is a short step to reading \(1 - p\) as \(P(H_1 \mid D)\): “p = .01, so there is a 99% chance the effect is real.”

Quiz statement 2 is the first step: reading p as \(P(H_0 \mid D)\). Statement 4 is both steps: reading \(1 - p\) as \(P(H_1 \mid D)\). Statement 5 reads p as \(P(H_0 \mid \text{significant result})\), the probability that a rejection of \(H_0\) is mistaken. All three treat a probability of data as a probability of a hypothesis.

4.3.2.1 A common variant on the fallacy: “the probability that the results occurred by chance”
The most common error in introductory textbooks identified by Cassidy et al. (2019), and one of the most common ways p-values are described in published articles, is a version of the same fallacy: “p = .03 means there is a 3% probability that the results occurred by chance.”
This reverses the definition. To say that the results occurred by chance alone is to say that the null model is true: there is no effect in the population, every other assumption holds, and any pattern in the data is due only to random sampling variation. But the p-value is calculated by assuming exactly that. It therefore cannot also be the probability that it is true. In the notation above, “the probability that chance alone produced the results” is \(P(H_0 \mid D)\), whereas the p-value is \(P(D \mid H_0)\) (Greenland et al., 2016). The American Statistical Association’s statement rules this interpretation out explicitly: p-values do not measure “the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone” (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016, p. 131).
The error often appears in a softer form that drops the word “alone”, such as “the probability that the result is due to chance” or “the probability that the difference is a fluke”. Greenland et al. (2016) note that this makes the statement more ambiguous but no less wrong. When assessing an article, it is worth comparing the wording to a correct version:

Incorrect: “There is a 3% probability that these results are due to chance.”
Correct: “If there were no true effect and the other assumptions of the test held, results at least as extreme as these would be expected 3% of the time.”

The correct version is longer and less satisfying, because it answers a less interesting question. That is precisely why the incorrect version is so common.



4.3.3 The replication delusion
Statement 6 reads 1 − p as the probability that a significant result would be obtained again if the study were repeated: p = .01, so a replication will succeed 99% of the time. Gigerenzer (2018) calls this the replication delusion. As noted above, 42 of the 70 academic psychologists surveyed by Oakes (1986) endorsed it (Cohen, 1994).
The probability that a replication will be significant has nothing to do with 1 − p. It is the replication’s statistical power, which depends on the true effect size and the replication’s sample size, neither of which the p-value tells us. Even in the most favourable case, where the observed effect is exactly the true effect, the probability of a significant exact replication is much lower than 1 − p suggests (Goodman, 1992):

An original result of p = .05 has only a 50% chance of being replicated at p < .05.
p = .01 has a 73% chance (not 99%).
p = .005 has an 80% chance.
p = .001 has a 91% chance.

In practice the true figures are usually lower, because significant results tend to overestimate the true effect: studies are more likely to cross the significance threshold, and to be published, when chance has inflated the observed effect. This is one reason that large-scale replication projects have found replication rates well below what the original p-values would suggest, as discussed in Section 4.4.1.
The replication delusion also connects to how p-values are distributed, which is the subject of the next section: the variability of p-values across exact replications is far greater than most researchers expect.


4.3.4 Alternatives to frequentist p-values: Bayes’ theorem
It is possible to get from \(P(D \mid H_0)\) to \(P(H_0 \mid D)\), and hence to \(P(H_1 \mid D)\), but only with additional information, using Bayes’ theorem:
\[
P(H_0 \mid D) = \frac{P(D \mid H_0)\,P(H_0)}{P(D \mid H_0)\,P(H_0) + P(D \mid H_1)\,P(H_1)}
\]
\[
P(H_1 \mid D) = 1 - P(H_0 \mid D)
\]
The p-value supplies only one of the terms, \(P(D \mid H_0)\). Two further things are needed that a significance test does not use:

The prior probability of each hypothesis, \(P(H_0)\) and \(P(H_1) = 1 - P(H_0)\): how plausible the null was before the data were collected.
The probability of the data if the alternative is true, \(P(D \mid H_1)\). This is harder than it looks, because \(H_1\) (“the effect is not zero”) covers every possible non-zero effect size, and \(P(D \mid H_1)\) is different for each. It can only be calculated by assuming a particular effect size or a distribution of plausible effect sizes.

If \(D\) is defined as “a significant result” rather than “data at least as extreme as those observed”, these terms become familiar: \(P(D \mid H_0) = \alpha\), and \(P(D \mid H_1)\) is the study’s statistical power at the assumed effect size. \(P(H_0 \mid D)\) is then the probability that a significant result is a false positive, which depends on power and on the prior probability of \(H_0\) as much as on \(\alpha\).
Frequentist methods treat hypotheses as fixed states of the world rather than as things with probabilities, so they deliberately leave the prior out, and with it any answer to \(P(H_1 \mid D)\).
This lesson and course is not on frequentist vs. Bayesian approaches to Null Hypothesis Significance Testing - I mention it only to give you some awareness of where pursuing these questions lead to and where you could learn more if you are interested (e.g., Kruschke, 2015; McElreath, 2020). The point is that p-values cannot, by themselves, give the answer to researcher’s most common or intuitive questions. So, researchers have three options:

Change our statistical methods to answer our chosen question.
Stick with frequentist p-values and reconsider the questions we are (implicitly) asking.
Keep misinterpreting p-values. [not this one, please]

4.5 Implications for trustworthiness assessment
Understanding what a p-value is, and how p-values behave, matters for trustworthiness assessment in four ways.
1. Interpretations of p-values are claims that can be checked. Reading p as the probability that \(H_0\) is true, treating a “marginally significant” result as support for a hypothesis, or treating a fragile p-value as strong evidence are all misalignments between an article’s results and its conclusions. Detecting them requires no access to data, only a careful reading of how the results are described. Chapter 7 covers common misinterpretations in detail.
2. A p-value is only as trustworthy as its null model. Because a p-value tests every assumption of the null model at once (Section 4.2.1.1), it is informative about \(H_0\) only to the extent that the other assumptions are credible: that the design was as described, that the analysis was planned rather than selected, and that the reported results are the ones that were obtained. Much of the rest of this book can be read as methods for checking those other assumptions.
3. Reported p-values can be checked against their test statistics. The bump just below .05 largely disappeared when Hartgerink et al. (2016) recalculated p-values from the reported test statistics, and one in eight articles contains a p-value whose inconsistency with its test statistic could change the conclusion (Nuijten et al., 2016). Unlike the distribution of p-values across a literature, this check works within a single article: every reported p-value can be recalculated from its test statistic and degrees of freedom. Chapter 10 covers how.
4. Distributions of p-values are flags, not verdicts. A set of results clustered just below (or just above) .05 is one of the fingerprints of a low-powered or biased literature, and it predicts poor replicability (Section 4.4.1).
For an individual article, however, this is a weaker signal. Any single p-value between .02 and .05 is entirely possible under honest research practices, whether because the study had modest power or simply by chance. The signal lies in patterns across many results: for example, when all of an article’s key results fall between .02 and .05, or when a multi-study article reports more significant results than its power could plausibly produce. In null-model terms (Section 4.2.1.1), such a pattern is evidence that some assumption of the null model has failed, and it points to the analysis and reporting assumptions rather than to \(H_0\) itself: true effects studied with adequate power do not produce clusters of fragile p-values, but selective analysis and reporting do. Even then, excess-significance tests depend on judgements about which experiments and tests bear on the same claim, and on power estimated from the same, possibly inflated, effect sizes. For example, van Boxtel and Koch (2016) argued that Francis (2014) had wrongly flagged their article by including experiments and tests that did not bear on their central hypothesis, and that similar inclusion decisions could affect 34 of the 44 articles he analysed. Francis (2016) replied that the tests he included were those the original authors had themselves used to support their theoretical claims, and that the appearance of excess success remained. Such patterns are therefore best treated as a reason to look more closely, using the methods in the rest of this book, rather than as a conclusion in themselves.

text:
5.3 When standarization is useful
The same construct is often measured with different scales, and different scales have different units. Depression, for example, is commonly measured with the BDI-II, which ranges from 0 to 63, the PHQ-9, which ranges from 0 to 27, and the HAM-D, which ranges from 0 to 52. A difference of 5 points between two groups means something different on each of them, so results from studies that used different scales cannot be compared or combined in their original units.
The plot below shows these three scales. Each row shows a scale’s logical range, with the distributions of a control condition and an intervention condition from a hypothetical trial of a treatment for depression drawn on it with the same SD. The distributions are beta distributions, rescaled to the range of each scale, with parameters calculated from the mean and SD by the method of moments; unlike normal distributions, they cannot run past the ends of the scale. The values are illustrative, not taken from particular studies. Lower scores mean less severe depression, so a negative difference favours the intervention. The panel underneath shows the difference between the two means on each scale, in whichever units are selected, with its 95% confidence interval. Each trial is assumed to have 60 participants per condition. The buttons re-express the same three trials in different units:

Scale units are the original units of each scale.
SD units divide every score by that sample’s standard deviation. This is the standardisation used by Cohen’s d and other standardised mean differences.

Switch between them and pay attention to what lines up and what does not.

standardisedDifferencePlot = unitsPlot({
  // illustrative values for a hypothetical trial: means are [control, intervention], with a common SD
  scales: [
    {name: "BDI-II", min: 0, max: 63, sd: 10, means: [28, 22]},
    {name: "PHQ-9", min: 0, max: 27, sd: 5, means: [15, 12.5]},
    {name: "HAM-D", min: 0, max: 52, sd: 6, means: [20, 16.7]}
  ],
  groups: [{name: "Control", colour: "#d9622b"}, {name: "Intervention", colour: "#2780e3"}],
  captions: [
    "In scale units, the three differences cannot be compared, because a point on one scale is not a point on another.",
    "In SD units, each difference is a Cohen's d, and the three can be compared. They are similar but not identical. The means themselves still do not line up, and neither do the ranges."
  ],
  n: 60,
  width
})






In scale points, the three trials appear to have found very different effects: 6 points, 2.5 points, and 3.3 points. In SD units, they are d = −0.60, −0.50, and −0.55, which is what we might expect from three trials of the same treatment. Standardising has not made the three results identical, and it should not: it has only put them in the same units so that they can be compared.
Standardising by the SD makes one thing comparable across scales: the unit. One SD is the same length on every scale, so in SD units the distributions on all three scales have the same width, which is what allows a mean difference of 6 points on the BDI-II to be compared with a mean difference of 2.5 points on the PHQ-9. It does not make anything else comparable. The three trials still have different means in SD units, and the scales still have different ranges. Note also that the unit is a property of the sample, not of the scale: a study that recruited a more homogeneous sample would have a smaller SD, and the same difference in scale points would become a larger standardised difference (see Section 5.4).

text:
6.1.1 Converting between them
Because the two differ only by a factor of \(\sqrt{N}\), each can be recovered from the other when the sample size is known. A 95% confidence interval for a mean can also be converted, because its half-width is the standard error multiplied by a critical value from the t distribution.

# standard error from standard deviation
se_from_sd <- function(sd, n) sd / sqrt(n)

# standard deviation from standard error
sd_from_se <- function(se, n) se * sqrt(n)

# standard deviation from the 95% confidence interval of a mean
sd_from_ci <- function(lower, upper, n) {
  se <- (upper - lower) / (2 * qt(.975, df = n - 1))
  se * sqrt(n)
}

se_from_sd(sd = 10, n = 25)

[1] 2

sd_from_se(se = 2, n = 25)

[1] 10

sd_from_ci(lower = 45.87, upper = 54.13, n = 25)

[1] 10.00534


In trustworthiness assessment these conversions are most useful in reverse: when it is unclear which statistic an article has reported, calculate what the SD would be under each interpretation and ask which of the two is plausible for that scale and that population.

section: 6.2 What happens when they are confused
text:
6.2 What happens when they are confused
Cohen’s d is the difference between two means divided by the standard deviation. If the number that is divided by is in fact a standard error, the denominator is too small by a factor of \(\sqrt{n}\), where n is the sample size of each group, and the effect size is too large by the same factor:
\[
d_{confused} = \frac{M_1 - M_2}{SD / \sqrt{n}} = d \times \sqrt{n}
\]
The error is therefore worse in larger studies. A true effect of d = 0.3 becomes 1.34 with 20 participants per group, 2.12 with 50 per group, and 3.00 with 100 per group. This is the opposite of what we usually expect from large studies, which are normally the ones whose estimates we trust most.
The plot below shows this. As in Section 8.2, it simulates 20,000 two-group studies at each sample size, each with a true standardised mean difference drawn from a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation τ. For each study it then calculates the effect size twice: once correctly, and once with the standard error of each group mistaken for its standard deviation. The lines show the median, and the bands show the 95% prediction intervals: the ranges within which 95% of studies’ observed effect sizes fall.

viewof cfMu = Inputs.range([0, 1.5], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "True (population) SMD μ"})
viewof cfTau = Inputs.range([0, 0.5], {value: 0.05, step: 0.05, label: "Between-study heterogeneity τ (SMD scale)"})
















{
  const series = [{name: "Correctly calculated", colour: "#8a8a8a"}, {name: "SE mistaken for SD", colour: "#d9622b"}]
  const data = simulateConfusedD(cfMu, cfTau)
  const rows = data.flatMap(d => [
    {n: d.n, series: series[0].name, lower: d.lower, median: d.median, upper: d.upper},
    // mistaking the SE of each group for its SD multiplies the effect size by the square root of the group size
    {n: d.n, series: series[1].name, lower: d.lower * Math.sqrt(d.n / 2), median: d.median * Math.sqrt(d.n / 2), upper: d.upper * Math.sqrt(d.n / 2)}
  ])
  return Plot.plot({
    width, height: Math.min(480, Math.max(320, width * 0.75)), marginLeft: 55, marginRight: 20, marginBottom: 45,
    x: {label: "Total N (both groups)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 38, ticks: [20, 50, 100, 250, 500]},
    y: {label: "Observed Cohen's d", labelAnchor: "center", grid: true, domain: [Math.min(-0.5, d3.min(rows, d => d.lower)), Math.max(3.2, d3.max(rows, d => d.upper))]},
    color: {domain: series.map(d => d.name), range: series.map(d => d.colour), legend: true},
    style: {fontSize: "13px"},
    marks: [
      Plot.frame({stroke: "currentColor"}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.5}),
      Plot.areaY(rows, {x: "n", y1: "lower", y2: "upper", fill: "series", fillOpacity: 0.25}),
      Plot.lineY(rows, {x: "n", y: "median", stroke: "series", strokeWidth: 2}),
      // the mean true SMD
      Plot.ruleY([cfMu], {stroke: "#2780e3", strokeDasharray: "6,4", strokeWidth: 2.5})
    ]
  })
}






Median (line) and 95% prediction interval (band) of an observed d, when it is calculated correctly and when the SE is mistaken for the SD. The dashed blue line shows the mean true effect μ.
Several things are worth noticing:

The correctly calculated effect sizes converge on the true effect as the sample size increases. The confused ones move further away from it.
The confused effect sizes are not slightly inflated versions of the correct ones. With the default settings, the median confused effect size is about 2 at a total sample size of 90 and nearly 5 at a total sample size of 500, when the true effect is 0.3.
Even a true effect of zero is affected. Set μ to 0: the confused effect sizes are still centred on zero, but they are spread over a range many times wider than the correct ones, so that large effects in both directions become common.
Small true effects are turned into effects that would be among the largest ever observed in most fields. An observed d of 2 or 3 is exactly what this error produces from an unremarkable true effect in a study of ordinary size.

The opposite error also occurs: a standard deviation is mistaken for a standard error, and is multiplied by \(\sqrt{n}\) on the assumption that it needs to be converted. This shrinks the effect size by a factor of \(\sqrt{n}\). It is harder to notice, because implausibly small effects attract less attention than implausibly large ones.

section: 6.3 Prevalence of SE/SD misuse in primary research
text:
6.3 Prevalence of SE/SD misuse in primary research
The error starts in primary research articles. Many articles report the standard error of the mean where a standard deviation is called for, that is, to describe the variability of the sample, and some do not say which of the two they are reporting. Either creates the conditions for the number to be misread later, by readers and by meta-analysts.

64%
of articles in three leading cardiovascular journals contained at least one instance of incorrect use of the standard error of the mean (Wullschleger et al., 2014).

Audits of the published literature in several fields of medicine have found the following:

Altman & Bland (2005) set out the distinction between the two statistics in a short and widely cited tutorial. They note that in one sample of articles, 14% failed even to identify which of the two was being reported.
Nagele (2003) found that 23% of articles in four anaesthesia journals inappropriately used the standard error of the mean to describe the variability of the sample.
Ko et al. (2014) found that 13.6% of articles in four obstetrics and gynaecology journals did so.
Wullschleger et al. (2014) found that 64% of articles in three leading cardiovascular journals contained at least one instance of incorrect use of the standard error of the mean.
Barde & Barde (2012) note one reason for the practice: authors sometimes prefer the standard error because it is smaller, which makes the data appear less variable.

Taken together, these audits suggest that somewhere between about 14% and 64% of primary research articles, depending on the field and on how the error is defined, report standard errors where standard deviations are appropriate or do not make clear which they are reporting.

section: 6.5 Checking for SE/SD confusion in trustworthiness assessment
text:
6.5 Checking for SE/SD confusion in trustworthiness assessment
The error is detectable more often than it is detected, because it leaves numbers that are implausible in several ways at once. When assessing an article or a meta-analysis:

Check what is labelled. Does every table and figure say whether the values after “±”, in parentheses, or shown as error bars are standard deviations, standard errors, or confidence intervals? Unlabelled values should not be assumed to be standard deviations.
Ask whether the reported SDs are plausible for the scale. Compare them with the range of the scale, with the SDs reported for the same measure in other studies of similar populations, and with each other across the tables of the same article. An SD that is a small fraction of what other studies report is more likely to be a standard error than a sign of an unusually homogeneous sample (see also Section 5.4).
Try the conversion. Multiply the suspicious value by \(\sqrt{n}\). If the result is a typical SD for that measure, the reported value was probably a standard error.
Look for SDs that shrink as groups get larger. Standard deviations should be similar across groups and subgroups of different sizes. Values that are systematically smaller in larger groups behave like standard errors.
Check whether the effect size is plausible. Standardised mean differences above about 2 or 3 are rare when calculated correctly (Section 8.2) and may not even be possible on a bounded scale (Section 8.1). Kadlec et al. (2023) traced most effect sizes above 3 in the meta-analyses they audited to this error.
Recalculate. Check that the reported means and SDs are consistent with the reported test statistics, p-values, and confidence intervals (see Chapter 10). A t-test calculated by the original authors from the raw data will not agree with an effect size calculated from standard errors that have been mistaken for standard deviations.
In a meta-analysis, inspect the forest plot. Look for studies whose effect sizes are far larger than the rest without having wider confidence intervals, particularly among the larger studies, and trace their extracted values back to the primary articles.

One consequence of the fact that the inflation grows with sample size is that this error does not look like the small-study effects that meta-analysts are trained to look for. Funnel plots and related methods are designed to detect the pattern in which small studies show the largest effects. Here it is the larger studies that are the most distorted.

text:
6.6 Test yourself

An article reports that anxiety scores on a 0–40 scale were lower in the intervention group (M = 14.2 ± 0.9, n = 64) than in the control group (M = 17.1 ± 1.0, n = 64), and does not say what the values after ± are. A meta-analysis that includes the study reports its effect size as d = −3.05. Mark each statement as true or false.

If the values after ± are standard deviations, the meta-analysis has calculated d correctly. TRUEFALSE
If the values after ± are standard errors, the SDs are about 7 to 8, and d is about −0.38. TRUEFALSE
Standard deviations of about 1 on a 0–40 scale would mean that nearly everyone in each group scored within a few points of each other. TRUEFALSE
The standard error would be the appropriate statistic for describing how variable the participants’ scores were. TRUEFALSE
If this study had recruited 256 participants per group and the same error had been made, the effect size in the meta-analysis would be less inflated. TRUEFALSE
Because the study is one of the larger ones in the meta-analysis, the error will have little influence on the pooled estimate. TRUEFALSE

title: 7  Misinterpretation methods ✎ Draft
text:
7.1 Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence
Many problems with published research are not errors in the numbers. The numbers are right, but the conclusions drawn from them do not follow. These are failures of claim–evidence alignment, and they are some of the easiest to detect, because the evidence needed to spot them is usually printed in the article itself.
This chapter starts with three misinterpretations of p-values that are common, consequential, and checkable:
The first two errors treat the significance threshold as a verdict about the world rather than a statement about the data, and both can usually be checked by calculating one additional number from what the authors report: a confidence interval for the effect in the first case, and a test of the difference in the second. The third ignores the threshold altogether while still borrowing its authority, and checking it usually requires going back to the original results, whether in the same article or in an article that is being cited.

title: 7  Misinterpretation methods ✎ Draft
text:
Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
Altman & Bland (1995)


7.1.1 The error
A p-value above .05 is often reported as if it showed that there is no effect: the treatment “did not work”, the groups “did not differ”, the variable “had no influence”, the two conditions were “equivalent”, or the trial was “negative”. Altman & Bland (1995) point out that the label “negative” wrongly implies that the study has shown that there is no difference, “whereas usually all that has been shown is an absence of evidence of a difference”. These are very different statements.
Recall from Section 4.2.1.1 that the p-value measures how compatible the data are with the null model. A p-value above .05 tells us that the data are not incompatible enough with the null model for us to reject it. It does not tell us that the null model is correct, because the same data are usually also compatible with many other effect sizes, including some that would be large and important. Which effect sizes the data are compatible with is exactly what the confidence interval shows. A nonsignificant result with a narrow interval around zero is informative. A nonsignificant result with a wide interval, stretching from a small harmful effect to a large beneficial one, tells us very little.
The plot below shows two hypothetical studies with exactly the same p-value, laid out as in the dance of the p-values (Section 4.4.0.1): each study’s p-value is on the right and its effect size estimate is on the left. Both studies are nonsignificant, and both would typically be reported in the same way: “there was no significant effect, p = .505”. The plot starts by showing only the p-values, and on this information the two studies are indistinguishable. Now click the button to reveal their effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals. Study A estimated the effect precisely, and its interval shows that any effect is at most very small (d between −0.06 and 0.12). Study B estimated it very imprecisely, and its data are compatible with anything from a moderate negative effect to a large positive one. The p-value is the same, but what the two studies tell us about the size of the effect is completely different. Only Study A comes close to providing evidence that there is no meaningful effect; Study B provides almost no information either way.

viewof showDs = {
  // a button that toggles between showing and hiding the estimates, styled like Inputs.button.
  // the value is stored on a wrapping div, because a button's own value property is always a string
  const button = html`<button class="btn btn-quarto">Show effect sizes and 95% CIs</button>`
  const view = html`<div>${button}</div>`
  view.value = false
  button.onclick = () => {
    view.value = !view.value
    button.textContent = `${view.value ? "Hide" : "Show"} effect sizes and 95% CIs`
    view.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}))
  }
  return view
}

  <div><div style="text-align: center; font-weight: 600;"><i>p</i>-value</div>${samePRight}</div>
</div>`

].map(d => ({...d, lo: d.est - 1.96 * d.se, hi: d.est + 1.96 * d.se, p: 2 * normCdf(-Math.abs(d.est / d.se))}))

  width: samePPanelWidth, height: 220, marginTop: 20, marginLeft: 65, marginRight: 15, marginBottom: 40,
  x: {label: "Effect size (d) and 95% CI", domain: [-1, 1.4], grid: true},
  y: {label: null, domain: samePPanelData.map(d => d.study), padding: 0.5},
  style: {fontSize: "12px"},

    Plot.frame({stroke: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.4}),
    showDs
      ? Plot.ruleY(samePPanelData, {y: "study", x1: "lo", x2: "hi", stroke: "#adb5bd", strokeWidth: 2})
      : Plot.text(["?"], {frameAnchor: "middle", fontSize: 40, fillOpacity: 0.3}),
    showDs ? Plot.dot(samePPanelData, {x: "est", y: "study", fill: "#adb5bd", r: 5}) : null,
    showDs ? Plot.text(samePPanelData, {x: "est", y: "study", text: d => `${d.est.toFixed(2)} [${d.lo.toFixed(2)}, ${d.hi.toFixed(2)}]`, dy: -14, fontWeight: 600, fontSize: 13}) : null
  ]
})
samePRight = Plot.plot({
  width: samePPanelWidth, height: 220, marginTop: 20, marginLeft: 15, marginRight: 15, marginBottom: 40,
  x: {label: "p-value", domain: [0, 1], grid: true, ticks: [0, 0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1], tickFormat: d => d === 0 ? "0" : String(d).replace(/^0/, "")},
  y: {label: null, domain: samePPanelData.map(d => d.study), padding: 0.5, axis: null},
  style: {fontSize: "12px"},
  marks: [
    Plot.frame({stroke: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0.05], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.4}),
    Plot.dot(samePPanelData, {x: "p", y: "study", fill: "#adb5bd", r: 5}),
    Plot.text(samePPanelData, {x: "p", y: "study", text: d => `p ${fmtP(d.p)}`, dy: -14, fontWeight: 600, fontSize: 13})
  ]
})































7.1.2 Why it matters
Most studies are too small to detect effects of the size that would matter. Altman & Bland (1995) describe a review by Freiman and colleagues of 71 “negative” trials published in the New England Journal of Medicine: only about 30% were large enough to have a 90% chance of detecting even a 50% difference in effectiveness between the treatments being compared. They also describe a trial comparing two treatments for variceal bleeding that recruited 100 patients when its own power calculation had called for 1,800. It concluded that the treatments were equally effective, even though the 95% confidence interval included differences in cure rates of up to 20 percentage points. In the most dramatic of their examples, only 5 of 24 trials of fibrinolytic treatment (mostly streptokinase) after heart attack had found a statistically significant reduction in mortality. An overview of all the trials found a clinically worthwhile 22% reduction, but the lack of significance in most individual trials had led to a long delay before this was appreciated.
The consequences are not limited to medicine. In the 1970s, many US states began to allow drivers to turn right at red traffic lights. Before-and-after studies of individual intersections and jurisdictions typically found no statistically significant increase in crashes, and this was taken to mean that the change was safe (Hauer, 2004). The individual studies were small, however. When Preusser and colleagues (1982) examined larger samples of crash data from several jurisdictions, they found that crashes involving pedestrians and right-turning vehicles at signalised intersections increased by between 48% and 107%, and those involving cyclists by between 72% and 82%. Hauer (2004) uses this case as one of his examples of “the harm done by tests of significance”.



7.1.3 How common is it?
Aczel et al. (2018) examined every nonsignificant result mentioned in the abstracts of articles published in 2015 in three psychology journals (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, and Psychological Science). In 72% of the 137 cases, the authors interpreted the nonsignificant result as evidence that the effect was absent. When Aczel et al. reanalysed the results using Bayes factors, fewer than 5% provided strong evidence for the null hypothesis over the alternative.

76–85%
of psychology articles that discussed a nonsignificant result interpreted it as evidence that the effect was absent, with no significant change between 2009 and 2021 (Murphy et al., 2025).

Murphy et al. (2025) coded the discussion sections of 599 articles in ten psychology journals. Between 54% and 62% of articles explicitly claimed that a nonsignificant result meant there was no effect in the population, while only 4–8% explicitly discussed the possibility that an effect existed but had not been detected.


7.1.4 Examples
Consider the following statements, of the kind that appear in results sections every day:

“A t test for independent samples on object-location memory showed no significant effect of priming, t(99) = .50, p = .616, d = .12.”
“The mean proportions of perseverative responses to these tones were very similar between participant groups … with no significant group difference, t(30) = .66, p = .51, d = .23.”

The first is phrased carefully: it reports only that the effect was not significant. The second goes further, describing the groups as “very similar”. Whether that is justified depends on what the confidence interval looks like, which the authors do not report. We return to this example below and calculate it.
A higher-profile example comes from a large online study of the “Reading the Mind in the Eyes” test, a measure of theory of mind (Baron-Cohen et al., 2015). Among typical adults, women scored higher than men on average. Among adults with autism, the authors reported that a two-way ANOVA “showed … an absence of a sex difference between males and females with autism (p = 0.907)”, and the article’s title describes a “complete absence of typical sex difference”. The p-value alone cannot support this claim. The question to ask is: do these data show that men and women with autism have equivalent average scores, or only that a difference was not detected? The answer depends on the precision of the estimate of the sex difference within the autism group, and on what size of difference would be considered meaningful. Note also that the claim that the sex difference is absent in autism but present in typical adults is a comparison between a significant and a nonsignificant effect, which is the second error covered in this chapter (Section 7.2).



7.1.5 What would count as evidence of absence?
A nonsignificant difference test cannot show that an effect is absent, but other analyses can provide evidence that an effect is absent, or at least too small to matter:

Confidence intervals. If the whole interval lies within a range of effects that everyone would agree are trivially small, the data are informative about the absence of a meaningful effect.
Equivalence tests. The two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure formalises this. The researcher specifies a smallest effect size of interest, which defines equivalence bounds (for example, d = −0.3 to 0.3), and then tests whether the effect is significantly greater than the lower bound and significantly less than the upper bound (Lakens, 2017; Lakens et al., 2018). If both tests are significant, the effect can be declared practically equivalent to zero. This corresponds to checking whether the 90% confidence interval lies entirely inside the bounds.
Bayes factors, which quantify the relative evidence for the null and alternative hypotheses (Section 4.3.4), as in the reanalysis by Aczel et al. (2018).

Crossing a difference test with an equivalence test gives four possible conclusions, not two:









Equivalence test p < .05
Equivalence test p ≥ .05




Difference test p < .05
An effect exists, but it is too small to matter
An effect exists and it may be meaningful


Difference test p ≥ .05
Evidence of absence of a meaningful effect
Inconclusive: absence of evidence



The plot below shows four hypothetical studies, one in each cell of this table. Each study’s estimate is shown with its 95% confidence interval, along with the p-value of the traditional difference test (is the effect different from zero?) and of the equivalence test (is the effect smaller than the smallest effect size of interest?). Try changing the equivalence bounds. Notice that Study 3 is nonsignificant under the difference test, just like Study 4, but it is compatible with everything from a moderate negative effect to a large positive one. Its nonsignificance is absence of evidence. Only Study 4 provides evidence of absence, and only relative to bounds that someone has to justify.

viewof eqBound = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.6], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Equivalence bounds (±d)"})







eqStudies = [
  {study: "Study 1", est: 0.60, se: 0.15},
  {study: "Study 2", est: 0.12, se: 0.04},
  {study: "Study 3", est: 0.10, se: 0.30},
  {study: "Study 4", est: 0.03, se: 0.06}
].map(d => {
  const pDiff = 2 * normCdf(-Math.abs(d.est / d.se))
  // two one-sided tests: the TOST p-value is the larger of the two one-sided p-values
  const pLower = 1 - normCdf((d.est + eqBound) / d.se)
  const pUpper = normCdf((d.est - eqBound) / d.se)
  const pEq = Math.max(pLower, pUpper)
  return {...d, lo: d.est - 1.96 * d.se, hi: d.est + 1.96 * d.se, pDiff, pEq,
          label: `${d.study}\ndifference p ${fmtP(pDiff)}\nequivalence p ${fmtP(pEq)}`}
})

Plot.plot({
  height: 360,
  marginLeft: 180,
  marginBottom: 45,
  marginRight: 20,
  x: {label: "Cohen's d with 95% CI", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 38, domain: [-0.8, 1.2]},
  y: {label: null, type: "point", domain: eqStudies.map(d => d.label), padding: 0.5, axis: null},
  style: {fontSize: "13px"},
  marks: [
    Plot.text(eqStudies, {x: -0.8, y: "label", text: "label", textAnchor: "end", dx: -10, lineHeight: 1.25}),
    Plot.rect([{}], {x1: -eqBound, x2: eqBound, fill: "#2780e3", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
    Plot.ruleX([-eqBound, eqBound], {stroke: "#2780e3", strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
    Plot.link(eqStudies, {x1: "lo", x2: "hi", y1: "label", y2: "label", stroke: d => colourFor(d), strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(eqStudies, {x: "est", y: "label", fill: d => colourFor(d), r: 6})
  ]
})
















md`Shaded region: equivalence bounds of *d* = ±${eqBound.toFixed(2)}. Green: significant difference from zero. Blue: statistically equivalent to zero. Purple: both. Grey: neither (inconclusive).`







function colourFor(d) {
  const sigDiff = d.pDiff < 0.05, sigEq = d.pEq < 0.05
  return sigDiff && sigEq ? "#8e5bb5" : sigDiff ? "#3b9c6e" : sigEq ? "#2780e3" : "#8a8a8a"
}
function fmtP(p) {
  if (p < 0.001) return "< .001"
  return "= " + p.toFixed(3).replace(/^0/, "")
}
function normCdf(x) {
  // Abramowitz & Stegun 7.1.26
  const t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911 * Math.abs(x) / Math.SQRT2)
  const erf = 1 - (((((1.061405429 * t - 1.453152027) * t) + 1.421413741) * t - 0.284496736) * t + 0.254829592) * t * Math.exp(-x * x / 2)
  return x >= 0 ? 0.5 * (1 + erf) : 0.5 * (1 - erf)
}
























7.1.6 Checking for this error in trustworthiness assessment

Find the claims of absence. Look for phrases such as “no effect”, “did not differ”, “no difference”, “unaffected”, “unrelated”, “similar”, “equivalent”, “comparable”, “failed to replicate”, “no evidence that”, and “negative trial”, particularly in abstracts and discussions, where results are summarised most loosely.
Find the evidence for each claim. Is the claim supported by an equivalence test, a Bayes factor, or a confidence interval that excludes meaningful effects? Or only by p > .05?
If no interval is reported, reconstruct one. A confidence interval can usually be calculated from the reported test statistic, degrees of freedom, and group sizes (see Chapter 10).
Ask what size of effect would matter, and whether the interval rules it out. If the authors reported a power analysis, the effect size they powered the study for is a natural benchmark: if the interval includes it, the study cannot claim to have ruled it out.
Ask whether the argument depends on the absence claim. Claims of absence are often doing important work: that groups did not differ at baseline, that a treatment had no side effects, that a manipulation did not also change mood, or that an effect did not depend on participants’ awareness. They are also often convenient for the authors, which is a good reason to check them carefully.


7.1.6.1 Worked example
Take the second statement above: t(30) = .66, p = .51, d = .23, reported as showing that the two groups were “very similar”. Assuming equal group sizes of 16, we can reconstruct the 95% confidence interval for d from the t statistic using the noncentral t distribution:

# 95% CI for Cohen's d from an independent-samples t test, via the noncentral t distribution
ci_d_from_t <- function(t, n1, n2, conf = .95) {
  alpha <- 1 - conf
  df <- n1 + n2 - 2
  ncp_lower <- uniroot(function(ncp) pt(t, df, ncp) - (1 - alpha/2), c(t - 10, t + 10))$root
  ncp_upper <- uniroot(function(ncp) pt(t, df, ncp) - alpha/2, c(t - 10, t + 10))$root
  scale <- sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)
  round(c(d = t * scale, lower = ncp_lower * scale, upper = ncp_upper * scale), 2)
}

ci_d_from_t(t = 0.66, n1 = 16, n2 = 16)

    d lower upper 
 0.23 -0.46  0.93 


The data are compatible with anything from a moderate effect in one direction (d = −0.46) to a large effect in the other (d = 0.93). With 16 participants per group, the study had only about 28% power to detect a difference of d = 0.5. The groups may be very similar, but this study cannot tell us whether they are. The appropriate description is that the difference was not statistically significant and was estimated imprecisely.



7.1.7 Test yourself

A randomised trial with 20 patients per group compared a new analgesic with placebo and found no significant difference in pain scores, t(38) = 1.10, p = .28, d = 0.35, 95% CI [−0.28, 0.97]. Mark each statement as true or false.

The trial shows that the drug does not reduce pain. TRUEFALSE
The data are compatible with the drug having no effect on pain. TRUEFALSE
The data are compatible with the drug having a large effect on pain. TRUEFALSE
The trial provides good evidence that the drug and placebo are equivalent. TRUEFALSE
To claim that the drug’s effect is too small to matter, the authors would need to specify what size of effect would matter and show that the data rule out effects that large. TRUEFALSE

title: 7  Misinterpretation methods ✎ Draft
section: 7.2 The difference between “significant” and “not significant” is not itself statistically significant
text:
7.2 The difference between “significant” and “not significant” is not itself statistically significant

The difference between “significant” and “not significant” is not itself statistically significant.
Gelman & Stern (2006)


7.2.1 The error
The second error involves comparing two results by comparing their p-values. One effect is significant and another is not, and this is read as showing that the two effects are different: the treatment worked in women but not in men; the effect was found in the original study but not in the replication; the intervention group improved but the control group did not; the effect appeared with one analysis but disappeared with another.
This does not follow. A claim that two effects differ is a claim about the difference between them, and it has to be tested directly, with a test of the difference or of the interaction. Gelman & Stern (2006) emphasise that this is not simply the familiar point that the .05 threshold is arbitrary, so that p = .049 and p = .051 are practically the same result. Rather, “even large changes in significance levels can correspond to small, nonsignificant changes in the underlying quantities”.


7.2.2 A simple example
Gelman & Stern (2006) illustrate this with two independent studies that estimate the same effect with the same standard error: 25 ± 10 and 10 ± 10. Study A is significant (p = .01); Study B is not (p = .32). The tempting conclusion is that A found an effect, B did not, and therefore the two studies found different results.
But the difference between the two estimates is 15, and the difference has its own, larger, standard error: \(\sqrt{10^2 + 10^2} \approx 14\). The test of the difference gives p = .29, which is no more significant than Study B on its own. Study A crossing the threshold while Study B does not could easily happen even if the two true effects were identical.

viewof estA = Inputs.range([-40, 60], {value: 25, step: 0.5, label: "Study A: estimate"})
viewof seA = Inputs.range([0.5, 25], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "Study A: standard error"})
viewof estB = Inputs.range([-40, 60], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "Study B: estimate"})
viewof seB = Inputs.range([0.5, 25], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "Study B: standard error"})






























gsRows = {
  const seDiff = Math.sqrt(seA ** 2 + seB ** 2)
  return [
    {name: "Study A", est: estA, se: seA, colour: "#3b9c6e"},
    {name: "Study B", est: estB, se: seB, colour: "#8a8a8a"},
    {name: "A − B", est: estA - estB, se: seDiff, colour: "#d9622b"}
  ].map(d => {
    const p = 2 * normCdf(-Math.abs(d.est / d.se))
    return {...d, lo: d.est - 1.96 * d.se, hi: d.est + 1.96 * d.se, p,
            label: `${d.name}\n${fmtNum(d.est)} ± ${fmtNum(d.se)}, p ${fmtP(p)}`}
  })
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 280,
  marginLeft: 160,
  marginBottom: 45,
  marginRight: 20,
  x: {label: "Estimate with 95% CI", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 38, domain: [gsXmin, Math.max(45, ...gsRows.map(d => d.hi))]},
  y: {label: null, type: "point", domain: gsRows.map(d => d.label), padding: 0.5, axis: null},
  style: {fontSize: "13px"},
  marks: [
    Plot.text(gsRows, {x: gsXmin, y: "label", text: "label", textAnchor: "end", dx: -10, lineHeight: 1.25}),
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
    Plot.link(gsRows, {x1: "lo", x2: "hi", y1: "label", y2: "label", stroke: "colour", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(gsRows, {x: "est", y: "label", fill: "colour", r: 6})
  ]
})
















gsXmin = Math.min(-10, ...gsRows.map(d => d.lo))

function fmtNum(x) {
  return Number.isInteger(x) ? String(x) : x.toFixed(1)
}















The plot starts with Gelman and Stern’s numbers. The key feature is the third row, which shows the difference between the two studies and its confidence interval. Whether each study’s interval excludes zero tells us nothing about whether the studies differ from each other. Only the interval for the difference tells us that. Try moving Study B’s estimate to see how far apart the two estimates have to be before the difference becomes significant, and then try shrinking both standard errors.
Gelman & Stern (2006) add a third study with a much larger sample, which estimates the effect as 2.5 ± 1.0. This study is exactly as significant as Study A (p = .01). Judged by significance alone, it “replicates” Study A. But its estimate is ten times smaller, and the difference between A and this study is significant (22.5 ± 10.0, p = .03). Its estimate is much closer to that of Study B, the “failed” study. Set Study A to 25 ± 10 and Study B to 2.5 ± 1 to see this. Comparing significance levels can therefore mislead in both directions: it can make results that do not differ look different, and results that do differ look the same.
A related point concerns overlapping confidence intervals. Checking whether two intervals overlap is not a test of their difference either. Two independent estimates with the same standard error whose 95% intervals just touch differ with p ≈ .006, and intervals that overlap moderately can still differ significantly. Researchers are not good at judging this by eye (Belia et al., 2005). When in doubt, calculate the difference.


7.2.3 Where it appears
The error can occur wherever two results are compared, including:

Subgroups. The effect is significant in one group (women, younger adults, patients) but not another, and the authors conclude that the effect is specific to that group, without testing the interaction.
Conditions within a study. The intervention group improved significantly from baseline and the control group did not, so the intervention is declared effective, without comparing the change between groups. Nieuwenhuis et al. (2011) illustrate this and related forms of the error.
Predictors. Gelman & Stern (2006) discuss an influential finding that men’s sexual orientation was significantly associated with the number of older brothers but not with the number of older sisters, which was widely reported as showing that only older brothers mattered. The two coefficients were never compared, and Gelman and Stern suspect, from the published figures, that the difference between them was not significant.
Series of estimates. In another of their examples, a study of the effects of electromagnetic fields at many different frequencies grouped the frequencies by whether their effects were significant, and interpreted the groups as reflecting different underlying processes. Plotting the estimates with their standard errors showed a fairly consistent effect across frequencies, with the apparent structure attributable to sampling variability.
Analytic choices. An effect is significant with one outlier exclusion rule or covariate set but not another, and this is taken as showing that the choice changes the result.
Original studies and replications, covered below.

Moran et al. (2021) provides an example of the analytic choice type, from a registered replication report of a study of whether attitudes can be learned from stimulus pairings that participants are not aware of. The answer depended on how “unaware” participants were defined. Excluding participants using the original study’s awareness criterion, the pooled effect was g = 0.12, 95% CI [0.05, 0.20]; using an alternative criterion, it was g = 0.03, 95% CI [−0.06, 0.13]. Does the exclusion criterion change the result? The two intervals cannot answer this question on their own. Answering it requires an estimate of the difference between the two effects and its uncertainty, and because the two analyses share many of the same participants, that requires an analysis that accounts for the overlap rather than the simple formula used above.


7.2.4 How common is it?

50%
of the neuroscience articles that compared two effects in a way that invited this error made it: 79 of 157, among 513 articles in five top journals (Nieuwenhuis et al., 2011).

Nieuwenhuis et al. (2011) reviewed 513 behavioural, systems, and cognitive neuroscience articles published in Science, Nature, Nature Neuroscience, Neuron, and The Journal of Neuroscience. Of the 157 articles in which the authors compared two effects in a way that could lead to the error, 78 used the correct procedure (testing the difference or interaction) and 79 used the incorrect one. An additional analysis suggested that the error was even more common in cellular and molecular neuroscience. Their article is short and has a clear illustrative figure showing the common forms of the error, making it a good companion reading to Gelman & Stern (2006).


7.2.5 Checking for this error in trustworthiness assessment

Find the comparative claims. Look for phrases such as “but not”, “only in”, “specific to”, “selectively”, “moderated by”, “depended on”, “disappeared when”, “was eliminated”, “was stronger in”, and “failed to replicate”.
Check whether the difference was tested. Is there a test of the interaction, the moderation, or the difference between the estimates? If the claim rests only on one p-value being below .05 and another being above, the claim is not supported as stated.
If the estimates are independent, test the difference yourself. For two independent estimates with standard errors, the difference is tested with \(z = (b_1 - b_2) / \sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2}\). If only a 95% confidence interval is reported, the standard error can be approximated as its width divided by 3.92.
If the estimates are not independent, for example two outcomes measured in the same participants, two coefficients in the same regression model, or two analyses of overlapping samples, this formula is not valid, because it ignores the covariance between them. Note that the difference was not tested and that it cannot be reconstructed from the reported information.


# test of the difference between two independent estimates
diff_test <- function(est1, se1, est2, se2) {
  diff <- est1 - est2
  se_diff <- sqrt(se1^2 + se2^2)
  z <- diff / se_diff
  round(c(diff = diff, se = se_diff, z = z, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))), 3)
}

# approximate standard error from a 95% confidence interval
se_from_ci <- function(lower, upper) {
  (upper - lower) / (2 * qnorm(.975))
}

# Gelman and Stern's example
diff_test(est1 = 25, se1 = 10, est2 = 10, se2 = 10)

  diff     se      z      p 
15.000 14.142  1.061  0.289 




7.2.6 Implications for replication
The same logic applies to replications. It is common to judge whether a replication “succeeded” by whether it was significant, and whether it “failed” by whether it was not. This compares significance levels, and has both of the problems described above. A nonsignificant replication does not show that the original and replication results differ, and a significant replication does not show that they agree.
There is a further problem. The precision of any test of the difference between an original study and its replication is limited by the less precise of the two, which is usually the original. Morey & Lakens (2016) argue that because original studies in psychology are often so small, many published results are effectively unfalsifiable by replication: even a replication with an enormous sample cannot show that its result differs from the original’s.
Consider an original study with 10 participants per group that found p = .03, corresponding to d = 1.05, 95% CI [0.12, 1.99]. Suppose a replication with 5,000 participants per group finds d = 0.20, 95% CI [0.16, 0.24]. The replication is highly significant, so by the criterion of significance it “succeeded”. Yet its estimate is one fifth of the original, and the test of the difference between them is not significant:

diff_test(est1 = 1.05, se1 = se_from_ci(0.12, 1.99),
          est2 = 0.20, se2 = se_from_ci(0.16, 0.24))

 diff    se     z     p 
0.850 0.477 1.780 0.075 


The replication was not the problem. Because the original’s standard error is almost 0.48, the difference between the two studies would have to be about 0.94 standard deviations before it could reach significance, however large the replication. The original study was too imprecise to tell us much about the size of the effect, and so it is also too imprecise to be contradicted. In trustworthiness assessment, this is a reason to focus on effect size estimates and their precision, and to be cautious of any conclusion, from the original authors or from replicators, that rests on whether results fell on the same side of .05.


7.2.7 Test yourself

An article reports that a memory training programme improved recall in younger adults, p = .01, but not in older adults, p = .20. The abstract concludes that “the benefits of memory training are limited to younger adults”. Mark each statement as true or false.

The results show that the effect of training differs between younger and older adults. TRUEFALSE
To support the conclusion in the abstract, the authors would need to test the age group × training interaction. TRUEFALSE
If the 95% confidence intervals for the two age groups overlap, the effects cannot be significantly different. TRUEFALSE
If the two age groups are independent samples and the article reports the estimates and their standard errors, a reader can test the difference themselves. TRUEFALSE
If a large replication finds a significant effect of training in younger adults, it has found the same result as the original study. TRUEFALSE
