text:
7.3 Interpreting non-significant results as significant

7.3.1 The error
The first error in this chapter reads a nonsignificant result as showing that an effect is absent. This one reads it as showing that the effect is present. A result that did not meet the significance threshold, usually the authors’ own, is described, interpreted, or cited as if it had.
The error can enter at three points, and each is harder to detect than the one before:

In how the result is described. The result is reported as nonsignificant, but in language that suggests it nearly was significant.
In what the authors conclude from it. The result is reported as significant or as supporting the hypothesis when, by the conventional test, it was not.
In how other authors cite it. The original article reported its results accurately, but later articles describe it as having found something it did not.



7.3.2 Euphemisms for non-significance
The most visible form is the “marginally significant” result, covered in Section 4.4.2. Matthew Hankins’ list of over 500 phrases taken from the published literature, Still not significant, is the standard catalogue: “approaching significance”, “a trend towards significance”, “teetering on the brink of significance”, and so on. Such phrases are common: around 40% of p-values between .05 and .10 in APA journals were described as marginally significant (Olsson-Collentine et al., 2019).
From the point of view of trustworthiness assessment, the euphemisms are the least of the problems, because they are honest about the p-value. Their effect is to let the authors present a result as if it were support for their hypothesis while acknowledging that it is not. A reader who notices the phrase can see exactly what was found and judge it accordingly. The more serious cases are those where nothing in the wording signals that the result was nonsignificant.


7.3.3 Non-significant results reported as support
Sometimes a nonsignificant result is reported as significant, or as supporting a hypothesis, with no qualification. This can happen in several ways:

Undisclosed one-tailed tests. A one-tailed test halves the p-value. It can be legitimate when the direction of an effect was specified in advance, but when it is not disclosed, readers assume the conventional two-tailed test and read the result as stronger evidence than it is. When it is chosen after seeing the data, it simply moves the threshold from .05 to .10.
Incorrectly reported p-values. The reported p-value is below .05, but the p-value recalculated from the test statistic and degrees of freedom is above it. statcheck calls these decision errors, and they are more common for p-values reported as significant than for those reported as nonsignificant (Section 10.1.1).
Conclusions that outrun the results. The results section reports the test correctly, but the discussion or abstract describes the hypothesis as supported, or the effect as “replicated”, without mentioning that the key test was nonsignificant.


7.3.3.1 Example: the facial feedback hypothesis
Strack et al. (1988) is one of the most cited studies in social psychology, and a staple of introductory textbooks. In their Study 1, 92 participants rated the funniness of four cartoons while holding a pen either between their teeth (which forces a smile-like expression), between their lips (which prevents one), or in their nondominant hand. As predicted by the facial feedback hypothesis, the cartoons were rated as funniest in the teeth condition (M = 5.14), least funny in the lips condition (M = 4.32), and in between in the control condition (M = 4.77). The authors wrote that the results “clearly support the predictions”, and that the predicted pattern was “confirmed by a significant linear contrast, t(89) = 1.85, p = .03”.
Recalculating the p-value from the reported test statistic gives a different answer:

# two-tailed and one-tailed p-values for t(89) = 1.85
c(two_tailed = 2 * pt(-1.85, df = 89),
  one_tailed = pt(-1.85, df = 89)) |>
  round(3)

two_tailed one_tailed 
     0.068      0.034 


The reported p = .03 is the one-tailed p-value. We could find no statement in the article that the test was one-tailed. By the conventional two-tailed test, the result is p = .068: not significant. (statcheck would flag this result as a decision error, unless the words “one-tailed” or similar appeared in the text.)
The article’s Study 2 adds a second problem. It measured the same funniness ratings, and they did not differ between conditions (“all ps > .20”). The authors explained this by arguing that facial feedback should affect participants’ feelings of amusement, a new measure introduced in Study 2, but not their judgements of how funny the cartoons were, which was the dependent variable on which Study 1’s conclusions were based. Amusement ratings did show the predicted effect. The abstract describes Study 2’s results as having “replicated Study 1’s findings”.
None of this was hidden: every number needed to see it was in the article. But the article’s conclusions, its abstract, and its subsequent reputation are all based on the reading that Study 1 found a significant effect. When Wagenmakers et al. (2016) coordinated 17 preregistered direct replications of Study 1, involving a combined 1,894 participants, the meta-analytic difference between the teeth and lips conditions was 0.03 units on the 10-point scale (95% CI [−0.11, 0.16]), compared with 0.82 in the original. The replication effort was a response to the study’s influence, but that influence had rested from the start on evidence that was weaker than it was presented as being.



7.3.4 Non-significant results cited as significant
The final form of the error is the hardest to detect, because the article that makes it may be accurately reporting what it believes to be the literature. The original study reported a nonsignificant result accurately, but later articles cite it as if it had found an effect. Greenberg (2009) traced the citation network of a set of biomedical claims and documented several ways in which citation can create “unfounded authority” for a claim, including what he termed citation diversion: citing an article’s content but changing its meaning. Once a misdescription appears in a few influential reviews, later authors can repeat it from the reviews without reading the original.

7.3.4.1 Example: newborns’ preference for face-like patterns
Johnson et al. (1991) is a foundational study in developmental psychology, with over 2,000 citations on Google Scholar. Its first experiment replicated an earlier finding that newborns less than an hour old follow a moving schematic face further with their eyes and head than they follow a scrambled face or a blank head shape. Its second experiment, in 43 newborns, aimed to find out what about the face attracted them. It compared the schematic face with three other stimuli: a “config” stimulus of three dark squares in the positions of the eyes and mouth, the same three squares upside down (“inverse”), and a vertically scrambled arrangement of facial features (“linear”).
The results for eye movements were as follows. The schematic face was followed further than the inverse and linear stimuli (both p < .01), but only “almost significantly” further than config (p = .07). The comparisons between config and the two control stimuli, which are the comparisons that would show whether config itself was preferred, were not reported. From the figure, newborns followed the face by about 45° on average and each of the other three stimuli, config included, by roughly 38–40° (Wilkinson et al., 2025). Head-turning did not differ significantly between any of the stimuli. The authors’ own conclusion was that their results suggested “a face-like configuration of elements alone is insufficient” to explain the preference: some characteristics of the facial features also seemed to matter.
That is not how the study came to be cited. In a theoretical article published the same year, two of the same authors (Morton & Johnson, 1991) proposed that newborns have an innate face-detection mechanism, CONSPEC, and needed to specify what information it contained. They reasoned that because their experiments had not been able to distinguish the face from the config stimulus, the simplest hypothesis was that CONSPEC’s representation of a face resembles config. In other words, the nonsignificant difference between face and config (p = .07) was treated as evidence that the two were equivalent, which is the first error in this chapter (Section 7.1), and this equivalence was then used to infer that config would be preferred over controls, even though that preference was not supported in the same experiment. Note that the reasoning also inverts the roles of the stimuli: config was a candidate face-like stimulus being tested, not a control against which the face was being compared.
Wilkinson et al. (2025) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies comparing newborns’ attention to face-like and non-face-like stimuli, and traced how Johnson et al. (1991) has been cited. Of the ten most prominent review articles from 2024–2025 that cited it, nine cited it as showing a general inborn face preference, and seven attributed to it a preference for three-blob config-like stimuli. Widely used textbooks present it as showing that three-blob stimuli are sufficient to produce the preference, and many articles explicitly cite it as showing a preference for config over its inversion: a comparison it did not report, between two stimuli whose means were almost identical. A 2025 retrospective by Valenza and colleagues, quoted by Wilkinson et al. (2025), describes the second experiment as having shown “for the first time” that the configuration of features alone is sufficient to trigger the preference within hours of birth, which is the opposite of what the original authors concluded. Because config was believed to be preferred at birth, it became the standard stimulus in later research on newborns, fetuses, adults, autistic people, and computational models, and later results using it in days-old infants were interpreted as continuous with an inborn preference.
Wilkinson et al. (2025) are careful to say that their results do not show that there is no inborn face preference, and that the aim is not to fault individual authors for a misattribution that has become widespread. The point for trustworthiness assessment is that a claim’s support in the literature can be much weaker than its citation count suggests. A citation is a claim about what another article found, and like any claim it can be checked.



7.3.5 Checking for this error in trustworthiness assessment

Look for euphemisms. Phrases such as “marginally significant”, “approaching significance”, “a trend towards”, and “did not quite reach significance” signal that a result was nonsignificant. Check whether the conclusions treat it as if it were significant.
Recalculate the key p-values. For the results that the article’s conclusions depend on, recalculate the p-value from the test statistic and degrees of freedom, for example using statcheck (Section 10.1.1). If a reported p-value is half the recalculated two-tailed value, the test was probably one-tailed. Check whether this was disclosed, and whether the direction of the effect was specified in advance, for example in a preregistration.
Compare the abstract and discussion with the results. Words such as “supported”, “confirmed”, “demonstrated”, and “replicated” should correspond to tests that met the threshold the authors set. Check in particular whether a later study’s nonsignificant result on the original outcome has been replaced by a significant result on a different one.
Check the comparison that matters. Make sure the test that was significant is the test that the claim requires. In Johnson et al. (1991), the claim that config is preferred requires comparing config with the control stimuli, not comparing the face with them.
Read the cited original. When an important claim rests on a citation, particularly to a classic or foundational study, read the original results rather than relying on how the citing article, or a review, describes them. Check what was found, in which comparison, and what the original authors concluded.



7.3.6 Test yourself

An article’s abstract states that “consistent with our hypothesis, participants in the gratitude condition reported greater wellbeing than controls”. The results section reports “t(78) = 1.70, p = .047”. The article does not mention one-tailed tests or a preregistration. Mark each statement as true or false.

The reported p-value is consistent with a two-tailed test of t(78) = 1.70. TRUEFALSE
The reported p-value is consistent with a one-tailed test of t(78) = 1.70. TRUEFALSE
If the test was one-tailed, the authors should have said so, and readers should ask whether the direction was specified before the data were seen. TRUEFALSE
A result described as “approaching significance (p = .08)” provides good support for the hypothesis. TRUEFALSE
If a widely cited review states that a classic study found an effect, it is safe to assume that the classic study reported a significant test of that effect. TRUEFALSE

11.1 Granularity
Imagine a study where two participants are asked their age in years, and the article reports “mean age = 23.16”. Why is this result impossible?
Ages in years have to be whole numbers (integers), and the mean of two integers must end in either “.00” or “.50”. Put another way, the reported mean is inconsistent with the underlying data being integer and the sample size being 2.
This is the core of granularity methods: The granularity of the underlying data (e.g., integer data from Likert scales) means that summary statistics based on them (e.g., means and standard deviations) also have granularity, where only some numbers are mathematically possible.
Granularity methods are tests of possibility: they ask whether a reported value can exist at all, given what the article says about the data, not whether it is surprising. They need only what is printed: the summary statistics, the sample size, and a description of how the variable was measured. This chapter covers the two most widely used. GRIM (Section 11.2) checks a mean against its sample size, and GRIMMER (Section 11.3) adds the SD.

11.2 GRIM: Testing consistency among N/M/integer data
The GRIM test (granularity-related inconsistency of means) was introduced by Brown & Heathers (2017). The {scrutiny} package (Jung, 2026) implements GRIM and the other tests in this chapter.

11.2.1 How GRIM works
GRIM checks a reported mean in three steps. Take the age example from Section 11.1, a mean of 23.16 from 2 participants.

Multiply the reported mean by the sample size to get the implied sum: 23.16 × 2 = 46.32.
The scores are whole numbers, so their sum must be one too. Take the whole numbers on either side of the implied sum: 46 and 47.
Divide each by the sample size and round to the reported number of decimals: 46/2 = 23.00 and 47/2 = 23.50. If neither result matches the reported mean, the mean is inconsistent with the sample size, as 23.16 is here.

When each participant’s score is itself the average of several items, the sample size is replaced by N × items (Section 11.2.3). A mean that falls exactly halfway between two reported values can be rounded more than one way, which the test has to allow for (Note 11.1).


11.2.2 Visualising GRIM
Use the plot below to see which means can pass GRIM. Each square is a mean as it would be printed to the chosen number of decimals, and the row covers every such mean near the one you enter. The zoom setting chooses how far the row reaches on either side of it: 1 at low zoom, 0.5 at medium, and 0.25 at high. The rounding setting chooses what happens to a mean that falls exactly halfway between two reported values: it may be rounded either up or down, or only up (Note 11.1). Leave the number of items averaged at 1 unless each participant’s score is the mean of several items. A square is black if some set of N whole numbers has that mean, and white if no set does. Typing a mean centres the row on it. Clicking or dragging in the row chooses a mean without moving the row. The chosen mean is circled in blue.

viewof grim1N = Inputs.range([2, 100], {label: "Sample size (N)", step: 1, value: 2})
viewof grim1Digits = Inputs.select([1, 2], {label: "Decimal places", value: 2})

Try the default values first. They are the age example from Section 11.1: a mean of 23.16 from 2 participants. The square for 23.16 is white, because the only attainable means nearby are 23.00 and 23.50. Almost every square is white, because only 2 of every 100 two-decimal means can come from 2 participants. Then raise N towards 100 and watch the white squares thin out and disappear, as the attainable means crowd together until every two-decimal mean is attainable (Section 11.2.5). Switch to one decimal place and the white squares are gone from N = 10 onwards. Finally, try a mean of 3.12 from 8 participants under each rounding setting. The only whole-number sum near 3.12 × 8 = 24.96 is 25, and the exact mean of 25/8 = 3.125 is reported as 3.12 only if halves can be rounded down (Note 11.1).


11.2.3 What counts as whole-number (integer) data
GRIM’s central assumption is that each participant contributes a whole number. The practical skill in using it is knowing when that holds, and what the effective sample size is.
Explicit single items. One Likert-type question, one count. The number of response options is irrelevant: it makes no difference whether answers run from 0 to 3 or from 1 to 100 (Brown & Heathers, 2017).
Implicit single-item scales. Many variables are whole numbers without being thought of as scales: age in years, number of children, years of education, number of sessions attended, days in hospital, number of correct trials, cigarettes per day. These are often the best targets in an article, because they appear in baseline tables for every group and nobody expects them to be checked.
Multi-item scales. Here the scoring method decides the granularity.

A sum score across k items is still a whole number for each participant. The mean of sum scores moves in steps of 1/N, as for a single item.
A mean score across k items can take any multiple of 1/k for each participant. The mean of mean scores moves in steps of 1/(N × k), so the scale behaves like a single item answered by N × k people. A 10-item scale with 20 participants has the granularity of a single item with 200, and GRIM at two decimals has nothing to say about it.

The “items” in GRIM is therefore easy to misread. It is not the number of items in the scale. It is the number of items averaged to make each participant’s score, before the sample mean was taken. That number is 1 for a single question, and for any variable that is already a whole number for each participant, such as age in years. It is also 1 for a sum score, however many items were added up, because each participant’s total is a whole number. It is greater than 1 only when each participant’s responses were averaged first and the sample mean was then taken over those averages, and it is then the number of items that were averaged. A 20-item questionnaire scored as a sum has 1 item for GRIM, and the same questionnaire scored as a mean has 20.
This number is an input to the test that has to be extracted from the article, and getting it wrong produces false alarms. Brown and Heathers describe making this mistake themselves: what they took for inconsistent means on a single item turned out to be correctly reported means of a multi-item composite. For subscales, the relevant number is the items in the subscale, not in the full questionnaire. In {scrutiny}, it is given through the items argument.

# impossible for one item answered by 20 people, possible for the mean of a 3-item scale
grim(x = 3.42, n = 20, digits_x = 2, items = 1)

[1] FALSE

grim(x = 3.42, n = 20, digits_x = 2, items = 3)

[1] TRUE


Data that look like whole numbers but are not. Age calculated from date of birth, response scales that allow half points, visual analogue scales, reaction times, body mass index, and any score that has been weighted, standardised, transformed, or imputed. A scale with half-point options behaves like a two-item scale (Brown & Heathers, 2017), and can be tested as one. The others cannot be tested.
Statistics that GRIM cannot test at all. Adjusted means, estimated marginal means, conditional means or predicted values from a regression or mixed model, and other model-based estimates are not simple averages of the observed scores, even when the scores are whole numbers.
Percentages. A percentage is a mean of zeros and ones multiplied by 100, so GRIM applies to it directly, with k = 1. A percentage reported to d decimals is a proportion reported to d + 2 decimals, so a percentage given to one decimal is testable for samples of up to 999 (Brown & Heathers, 2017). For example, 37.5% of 13 participants is impossible: 4 of 13 is 30.8% and 5 of 13 is 38.5%.
Missing responses within a scale. If some participants skipped some items, the number of responses behind a mean score is smaller than N × k, and the test’s grid is wrong. Brown and Heathers found this caused an inconsistency in only one of the articles they examined, partly because multi-item scales are rarely GRIM-testable in the first place.

Note 11.1: Rounding





The last example in Section 11.2.2, a mean of 3.12 from 8 participants, has no single answer. Its only candidate sum gives an exact mean of 25/8 = 3.125, which is reported as 3.13 by some software and 3.12 by other software. Rounding gets its own note because, once extraction errors are set aside, it is the main way that a correct value can be flagged as impossible.

11.2.3.1 Rounding conventions
Several conventions are in use for a value that falls exactly halfway between two reportable numbers.

Round half up (strictly, away from zero): 3.125 becomes 3.13. This is what most people were taught at school, and what SPSS and Excel do.
Round half to even: 3.125 becomes 3.12 and 3.135 becomes 3.14. This is the default in R and Python.
Round half down: 3.125 becomes 3.12. Rare as a deliberate choice, but it happens by accident, as described next.
Floating-point artefacts. Computers store most decimal numbers approximately. A number that looks like an exact half may be stored as very slightly less, and is then rounded down whatever the rule.


round(0.125, 2)  # an exact half in binary: rounded to the even digit

[1] 0.12

round(0.375, 2)  # an exact half in binary: rounded to the even digit

[1] 0.38

round(2.675, 2)  # stored as 2.67499999..., so rounded down

[1] 2.67


Two further practices are not conventions for halves but change the reported value more broadly.

Truncation: the extra decimals are cut off, so 3.458 is reported as 3.45. A reported 3.45 could then stand for anything from 3.450 up to just under 3.460. This happens when values are copied by hand from output, or when numbers are formatted as text.
Stepped rounding: a value is rounded once to an intermediate number of decimals and then again. Brown and Heathers found a real case when they obtained the data behind a set of inconsistent SDs: SPSS had displayed 1.2849 at its default three decimals as 1.285, and the authors had then rounded this by hand to 1.29. The correct two-decimal value is 1.28. Stepped rounding can move a value a full unit in the last decimal place, even when the original was not close to a half.



11.2.3.2 Rounding is an assumption of the test
Authors almost never say how they rounded. They may not know, and different parts of the same article may have been produced by different software. The rounding rule is therefore not a fact about the article that we can look up. It is an assumption that we bring to the test.
The conservative response is to count a value as consistent if any reasonable rounding of halves reproduces it. This is what Brown & Heathers (2017) did, and it is the default in {scrutiny} (rounding = "up_or_down"). The strict alternatives are available for comparison:

grim(x = 3.12, n = 8, digits_x = 2, rounding = "up_or_down")

[1] TRUE

grim(x = 3.12, n = 8, digits_x = 2, rounding = "up")

[1] FALSE

grim(x = 3.12, n = 8, digits_x = 2, rounding = "even")

[1] TRUE


Truncation can be allowed for in the same spirit, by also accepting any sum whose mean would be cut down to the reported value. Stepped rounding is harder. {scrutiny} does not accommodate it, and neither does any other GRIM implementation we know of. It should be kept in mind as a possible innocent explanation for a failure, particularly when the reported value is one unit above an attainable one. It is also an undisclosed and incorrect practice, so “the authors rounded twice” is still a finding about the article’s reporting, if a minor one.
The practical advice is to run the lenient test as the main analysis, because a false accusation of impossibility is the costlier error, and to report how the verdicts change under stricter rules. A value that only passes because a half was rounded down, in an article whose other values were rounded up, deserves a note.
The rounding of reported values also matters when they are used as inputs to other calculations, such as recomputing a p-value from rounded means and SDs. That is covered in Chapter 10.










NoteThe maths: GRIM





Stated formally: a mean reported to d decimals is GRIM-consistent if there is a whole-number sum S such that S / (N × items), rounded to d decimals, equals the reported mean. Here “items” means the number of items averaged to make each participant’s score before the sample mean was taken, not the number of items in the questionnaire. It is 1 for a single question, a whole-number variable such as age in years, and a sum score.
Without rounding
Let \(x_1, \dots, x_N\) be the scores of \(N\) participants on a single item, each a whole number. Their sum is a whole number,
\[S = \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \in \mathbb{Z},\]
and the mean is that sum divided by the sample size,
\[M = \frac{S}{N}.\]
So the exact mean must satisfy
\[N \times M \in \mathbb{Z}.\]
This is the whole of GRIM when the mean is known exactly: multiply the mean by the sample size and check that the result is a whole number. The attainable means form an evenly spaced grid,
\[\mathcal{G}_N = \left\{ \frac{S}{N} : S \in \mathbb{Z} \right\},\]
and the spacing of the grid, \(1/N\), is the granularity of the mean.
For a mean score across \(k\) items, each participant’s score is the mean of \(k\) whole numbers, \(y_i = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k} x_{ij}\). The sum of all \(N \times k\) responses is a whole number, so
\[M = \frac{S}{N k}, \qquad N k \times M \in \mathbb{Z},\]
and the granularity is \(1/(Nk)\). A \(k\)-item mean score from \(N\) participants has the same grid as a single item from \(Nk\) participants. A sum score across \(k\) items is a whole number for each participant, so it is the single-item case.
The minimum and maximum of the response scale appear nowhere in these expressions. They restrict the range of \(S\), to between \(N k \times \min\) and \(N k \times \max\), but not the spacing of the grid.
With rounding
Articles report the mean rounded to \(d\) decimals. Call the reported value \(\tilde{M}\), and let
\[\delta = \frac{1}{2} \times 10^{-d}\]
be half of one reporting step, so \(\delta = 0.005\) at two decimals. The reported value does not identify the exact mean. It identifies an interval \(I(\tilde{M})\) of exact values that would all have been reported as \(\tilde{M}\). Which interval depends on the rounding practice (Note 11.1).



Table 11.2: Exact means that are reported as \(\tilde{M}\) under different rounding practices, for positive values.









Rounding practice
Interval of exact means, \(I(\tilde{M})\)




Halves rounded up
\([\tilde{M} - \delta,\ \tilde{M} + \delta)\)


Halves rounded down
\((\tilde{M} - \delta,\ \tilde{M} + \delta]\)


Halves rounded either way (lenient)
\([\tilde{M} - \delta,\ \tilde{M} + \delta]\)


Truncation
\([\tilde{M},\ \tilde{M} + 2\delta)\)


Stepped rounding through \(d + 1\) decimals, halves up
\([\tilde{M} - 1.1\delta,\ \tilde{M} + 0.9\delta)\)






The reported mean is GRIM-consistent if at least one attainable mean lies in the interval:
\[\mathcal{G}_{Nk} \cap I(\tilde{M}) \neq \varnothing
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\, S \in \mathbb{Z} : \frac{S}{Nk} \in I(\tilde{M}).\]
Multiplying through by \(Nk\) turns this into a question about whole numbers in an interval of sums. Under the lenient rule, the reported mean is consistent if and only if
\[\left\lceil Nk\,(\tilde{M} - \delta) \right\rceil \;\le\; \left\lfloor Nk\,(\tilde{M} + \delta) \right\rfloor,\]
where \(\lceil \cdot \rceil\) rounds up to the next whole number and \(\lfloor \cdot \rfloor\) rounds down. The left side is the smallest whole-number sum that is large enough, and the right side is the largest that is small enough. If the smallest exceeds the largest, no sum fits.
An equivalent form uses the whole number nearest to the implied sum. Writing \(S^{*}\) for \(Nk\,\tilde{M}\) rounded to the nearest whole number, the reported mean is consistent if and only if
\[\left| S^{*} - Nk\,\tilde{M} \right| \;\le\; Nk\,\delta .\]





11.2.4 Consistency rates under random means
Judging any GRIM result depends on one quantity. Suppose a reported value had nothing to do with any data, and was drawn at random from all the values that can be printed with d decimals. What is the probability that it passes GRIM?
This is the pass rate: the share of all printable values that the test would accept for a given design. A pass rate of 0.30 means that 30% of two-decimal values are attainable, so a wrong value picked at random has a 30% chance of slipping through. The fail rate is one minus the pass rate. Three properties make it useful.

It is a property of the design: the sample size, the number of items, the number of decimals, and the rounding rule. It does not depend on the reported value. It can be computed before looking at any results.
The fail rate is the test’s power against a random wrong value. A value with a fail rate of 0.72 is one where a wrong number would be caught 72% of the time. A value with a fail rate of zero cannot be caught at all.
It defines which values are informative. Only values with a fail rate above zero can tell us anything, whether they pass or fail.

function grimEndings(nk, d, rounding) {
  // which of the 10^d endings at d decimals some mean of nk whole numbers is reported as. only the decimal part of a
  // mean matters, so the sums S = 0 to nk - 1 cover every case. the arithmetic is in whole numbers, so that exact
  // halves stay exact: the mean S / nk is S x 10^d / nk reporting steps
  const scale = 10 ** d, reached = new Uint8Array(scale)
  const rules = {up_or_down: ["up", "down"], up_or_down_trunc: ["up", "down", "trunc"]}[rounding] ?? [rounding]
  for (let S = 0; S < nk; S++) {
    const num = S * scale, q = (num - (num % nk)) / nk, twice = 2 * (num % nk)
    for (const rule of rules) {
      // twice the remainder is above, below, or equal to nk when the mean is above, below, or exactly at a half
      const v = rule === "trunc" ? q
        : twice > nk ? q + 1 : twice < nk ? q
        : rule === "up" ? q + 1 : rule === "down" ? q : q % 2 === 0 ? q : q + 1
      reached[v % scale] = 1
    }
  }
  return reached
}

11.2.4.1 The cost of leniency
Every rounding practice that the test accommodates widens the band of exact values that count as a match, so more wrong values pass. The trade-off is unavoidable: a lenient test raises fewer false alarms and misses more errors.
To see its size, we work out the pass rate under different combinations of rounding rules. For each sample size, we take every mean that whole numbers can produce, round it under each rule with the {roundwork} package (which {scrutiny} uses for its own rounding), and count how many of the 100 possible two-decimal endings are reached. For the “up” and “up or down” rules, these counts are the same as the share of endings that {scrutiny}’s grim() accepts. We use the same function for the pass rates in the rest of the chapter.
Here we use the pass rate to compare three versions of the test.

Under the strict rule the pass rate is exactly N/100. Allowing halves to go either way makes no difference at most sample sizes, because exact halves only arise when the sample size is a multiple of 8. Where they do arise the effect can be large: at N = 40 the pass rate is 60% instead of 40%, and at N = 80 every value passes, so the lenient test already stops being informative there. Allowing truncation as well costs more, and at almost every sample size: the pass rate climbs about one and a half times as fast, and from about N = 67 nothing can fail. The exceptions are sample sizes that divide evenly into 100, such as 20, 25, and 50, where means have no further decimals to cut off.
The same idea carries over to the other tests. For percentages, the pass rate is about N / 10d+2. For GRIMMER, Figure 11.4 in Section 11.3 shows the joint pass rate for a random mean and SD, which is far lower than for GRIM alone in small samples. {scrutiny} reports the fail rate under the strict rule as the probability column of grim_map(), and grim_probability() returns it directly.
Is a random number the right comparison? The pass rate assumes that a wrong value is equally likely to be any printable value. Real wrong values are not like that. A typo usually changes one digit. A value copied from the wrong row is another real mean. People who invent numbers favour some final digits and avoid others. The uniform assumption is best treated as a reference point, not a model of how errors arise, and conclusions that depend on it should be checked against other reference distributions. The grim_sensitivity() function in {strait} does this for digit preferences.



11.2.5 When GRIM is uninformative
The most important practical fact about GRIM is where its pass rate reaches 100%. From that point every printable value passes, the test cannot fail, and a pass tells us nothing. The test can only fail when the attainable means are further apart than the reporting steps, which requires
\[N \times \text{items} < 10^{d}\]
where d is the number of reported decimals. With the usual two decimals, GRIM applies to fewer than 100 participants on a single item. At or above that, every two-decimal value is attainable and every mean passes. Brown and Heathers call variables below this limit GRIM-testable. Allowing halves to be rounded either way can end the test slightly earlier, at sample sizes that produce exact halves. At N = 80, for example, every two-decimal value passes (Section 11.2.4.1). The GRIM plot in Section 11.2.2 reports the test as uninformative in both cases.

NoteThe maths of when GRIM cannot be used





In units of the sum, the interval \(Nk \times I(\tilde{M})\) has width
\[2\,\delta\,Nk = \frac{Nk}{10^{d}}.\]
An interval of width 1 or more that includes at least one of its ends always contains a whole number. So whenever \(Nk \ge 10^{d}\), every reported value is consistent and the test cannot fail. This is the condition \(N \times \text{items} < 10^{d}\) given above.
When \(Nk < 10^{d}\), neighbouring attainable means are more than one reporting step apart, so each rounds to a different reported value. The \(Nk\) attainable means in any unit interval, such as from 3.00 up to 4.00, therefore account for exactly \(Nk\) of the \(10^{d}\) values that can be printed there. Under a strict rounding rule, the share of printable values that are consistent is
\[p = \frac{Nk}{10^{d}},\]
and the share that are inconsistent is \(q = 1 - p\). These are the pass rate and fail rate described in Section 11.2.4. Under the lenient rule, an attainable mean that falls exactly halfway between two printable values makes both of them consistent, so \(p\) is larger by one printable value for each such tie.
A percentage reported to \(d\) decimals is a proportion reported to \(d + 2\) decimals, with \(k = 1\). Everything above applies with \(d + 2\) in place of \(d\).





11.2.6 Interpreting a consistent result
A failure and a pass are not mirror images. A failure shows that something among the reported mean, the sample size, the description of the measure, and the rounding is not as stated (Section 11.5). A pass only shows that the mean was not caught, and what that is worth depends on how likely a wrong value would have been to be caught.
The pass rate answers this, because it describes the counterfactual of a value that has nothing to do with the data. Suppose a mean from 12 participants passes GRIM. A value picked at random would have passed only about 12% of the time, so the pass rules out most ways of being wrong. Now suppose a mean from 90 participants passes. A random value would have passed about 90% of the time, so the pass is almost exactly what we would expect whether the mean was correct or not. From 100 participants on, a pass carries no information at all.
A consistent result is therefore best reported as “not shown to be impossible”, together with its pass rate, and never as evidence that a value is correct. The same holds for a set of values: ten random values would all pass at N = 90 about a third of the time, but three would all pass at N = 12 less than once in 500 tries.

11.4 What large-scale applications have found

36 of 71
GRIM-testable psychology articles contained at least one mean that was inconsistent with its reported sample size (Brown & Heathers, 2017).

The only systematic application of GRIM to a sample of the literature that we know of is in the article that introduced it. Brown & Heathers (2017) searched the 2011–2015 issues of Psychological Science, the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, and the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology for articles containing the word “Likert”, and examined 260 of them. Of these, 189 (73%) had no GRIM-testable data, mostly because their samples were too large. In the remaining 71:

35 (49%) reported all testable means consistently.
15 (21%) had one or two inconsistencies that looked like typographical errors.
5 (7%) had a small number of inconsistencies that might affect the main results.
16 (23%) had a larger number of inconsistencies, often at several points in the article. In some of these, more than half of the testable values were inconsistent.

The authors requested the data for the 21 articles in the last two categories. They obtained data from eight authors, and a ninth provided enough information to check the means. Five authors refused, four promised data that did not arrive, and the rest could not be reached or did not reply. In all nine cases that could be checked, GRIM had identified at least one real problem, and three articles needed formal corrections.
The causes they found in these nine articles are instructive, because none of them is fraud and most are mundane: sample sizes that differed from those reported (in five of the nine cases), a spreadsheet formula that included the wrong cells, values copied incorrectly, the stepped rounding of SDs described in Note 11.1, and, in one case, an analysis error serious enough for the authors to issue a correction once they noticed it while preparing the data. In one case, Brown and Heathers had themselves made an error by overlooking that a measure was a multi-item composite.
The nine were the articles whose authors cooperated. The other twelve, whose authors refused the request for data, did not send it, or did not reply, were left unresolved in the published article. A later preprint by one of its authors reports what Brown and Heathers had concluded about them (Heathers, 2024). All twelve contained multiple inconsistencies, and three contained what the authors considered definite hallmarks of systematic data manipulation. These figures were removed from the 2017 article because they were judged “sufficiently speculative and controversial at the time of publication”. Taken together, they put the share of the 71 GRIM-testable articles with hallmarks of data manipulation at between 3 of 71 (4.2%) and 12 of 71 (16.9%). The range is wide for two reasons. A refusal to share data is not in itself evidence of manipulation, and the three clearest cases rest on the authors’ judgement of the reported values, without the data that would settle them.
Granularity tests also became known through case studies. GRIM and GRIMMER were among the tools used in the reanalysis of four articles from the Cornell Food and Brand Lab (Zee et al., 2017).

False negatives have a different set of causes, most of which cannot be fixed.

The test cannot fail. When N × items is 100 or more at two decimals, GRIM passes everything.
Chance. A wrong value can land on an attainable one. For a wrong value picked at random, the probability is the pass rate (Section 11.2.4).
Leniency. Every accommodated rounding practice lets more wrong values through.

The asymmetry between the two outcomes is the main thing to take from this section. A failure is strong evidence that something is misreported, provided the checks in Table 11.3 have been made, and no evidence about what or why. A pass is weak evidence of anything. Brown and Heathers make the same point: the number of GRIM failures in an article is a conservative estimate of the number of errors.

title: 11  Granularity methods ✎ Draft
text:
11.6 Other granularity methods: GRIM-U
Granularity is not restricted to means and SDs of integer data. Any statistic that is calculated from a finite number of discrete outcomes can take only a finite set of values, so many other granularity tests could in principle be developed. Means and SDs were simply the first applications.
GRIM-U (Heathers & Grimes, 2025) applied the principle to the Mann-Whitney U test. It relies on the granularity not of the data, which could be continuous, but of the ranks that the test calculates, and so of its U statistic and p-value. The test ranks all the observations from two groups and counts, for every pair made of one observation from each group, which group’s member ranks higher. The U statistic is that count.
Rank tests are a good target because they are used where samples are small and data are not normal: animal studies, pilot trials, and small clinical samples. These are the conditions under which granularity is coarse and the test can fail.
Hussey subsequently formalised an analytic form of GRIM-U, which does not need to enumerate every possible ranking, and implemented it in the {analyticgrimu} R package (Hussey, 2026). For the moment, this chapter does not attempt to explain analytic GRIM-U in any detail, or examine the sample sizes at which its results are informative, or consider the complexities of (assumed) maximum number of ties, etc. GRIM-U is still in early development; this content might be added later. Right now, the point is merely to highlight that other granularity methods do or could exist, and that this is an area of active research in methods development.

11.6.1 Additional assumptions
GRIM-U needs more assumptions than GRIM, because a Mann-Whitney p-value can be calculated in several ways. Software may use the exact distribution or a normal approximation, with or without a continuity correction, and with or without a correction for ties. Exact p-values are also defined in more than one way. Sidedness matters too. {analyticgrimu} treats these as GRIM treats rounding: a reported result passes if any modelled convention reproduces it.
Ties are the largest source of leniency. Ties shrink the variance of U, so the same U can give a range of p-values depending on how heavily tied the data were. The package computes that range exactly and accepts anything inside it, so a correctly reported result from tied data is never flagged. The price is that the default test is weak. Checking a p-value on its own will almost never flag anything, and detection is one-sided: a p-value that is too large for its U can be caught, but one that is too small can always be explained by supposing more ties.
Two features recover some of the lost ground. If the measure is known to be continuous, or to have a known number of scale points, this can be stated, and the accepted range narrows. The share of three-decimal p-values that are attainable for two groups of six falls from 94% when any ties are allowed to 7% when there are none.

grimu_saturation(n1 = 6, n2 = 6, decimals = 3)

[1] 0.9380619

grimu_saturation(n1 = 6, n2 = 6, decimals = 3, ties = "none")

[1] 0.06993007


These options are safe in one direction only. If the data were more tied than was assumed, correct results will be flagged, so it is better to err towards allowing ties. The function also reports the minimum amount of tying that a consistent explanation would require. A result that is only possible if half the sample shares one value is unremarkable for a single five-point item and not credible for a reaction time.
One coverage gap remains. Some software computes an exact permutation p-value conditional on the observed pattern of ties, which cannot be reconstructed from the group sizes. A failure against a result produced that way may reflect the gap and not an error.
Heathers & Grimes (2025) demonstrate GRIM-U on four published medical studies. No large-scale applications of GRIM-U have been conducted to date.

A possibility test. GRIM asks whether a reported mean can exist at all, given the sample size and whole-number data. It does not ask whether the result is surprising or unlikely, which is what plausibility tests do. See the chapter on organising principles.
True. That is the whole test: some whole-number sum, divided by N × items and rounded, must give the reported mean (Section 11.2).
True. GRIMMER adds a second check, on the sum of the squared scores, which must be a whole number with the same parity (odd or even) as the sum of the scores. An SD can fail this check even when the mean is fine (Section 11.3).
False. A failure shows that the mean, the sample size, the description of the measure, and the rounding cannot all be as stated. It does not say which one is wrong, or why. In the largest application of GRIM, the causes found were mundane: wrong sample sizes, spreadsheet errors, values copied incorrectly, and stepped rounding (Section 11.4).
False. 12.10 × 10 = 121, a whole number, so the mean is GRIM-consistent. GRIM only looks at the grid of attainable means. It knows nothing about the scale’s minimum and maximum.
False. On a 1–7 scale, no mean can be above 7. The value is impossible, but for a reason GRIM cannot see. Checks that use the scale’s limits are the subject of the next chapter, on bounds methods.
1. Each participant’s sum is a whole number, so a sum score behaves like a single item, however many items were added up. The number of items only enters the test when each participant’s answers are averaged first (Section 11.2.3).
False. With each participant’s score averaged over 12 items, the mean moves in steps of 1/(15 × 12) = 1/180. That is finer than the two-decimal reporting steps, so every two-decimal mean is attainable and the test cannot fail.
False. Model-based estimates such as estimated marginal means, covariate-adjusted means, and predicted values are not simple averages of the observed scores. Testing them with GRIM produces false positives (Table 11.3).
False. The only candidate sum is 25, and 25/8 = 3.125 exactly. Rounded half up, that is 3.13, so 3.12 fails. It passes only if halves can be rounded down, which is why the lenient rule counts it as consistent (Note 11.1).
False. With a single item and 100 or more participants, attainable means are no further apart than the reporting steps of 0.01, so every two-decimal mean passes. The test is uninformative here (Section 11.2.5).
90%. With two decimals and fewer than 100 participants on a single item, about N% of all printable values are attainable. So a value made up at random would pass 90% of the time (Section 11.2.4).
False. A test that 90% of random numbers would pass is weak evidence of anything. The pass is what we would expect if the mean were correct, and also very nearly what we would expect if it were not. A consistent result at large N should be read as “not shown to be impossible”, not as “shown to be correct” (Section 11.2.6).
True. At N = 12, a random value would pass only about 12% of the time, so a pass rules out more ways of being wrong. The informativeness of a pass depends on how often a wrong value would have failed.
True. GRIMMER’s check on the SD stays demanding at larger samples when the SD is small. title: 22  Forensic meta-science methods require validation ✎ Outline
text:
22.1 Proposed standard
Many forensic meta-science methods have been developed by non methodologists. This is probably not accidental: maybe it required some outside thinkers to develop the agonizingly simple math that GRIM is based on.
But, now that these methods have been conceived of, they need to be validated. There is an asymmetric reputational risk here: if we use these methods to determine that other research is untrustworthy, and it is in fact our methods that are untrustworthy, we are going to look quite silly. This is where the (quantitative) forensic meta-science research community is currently falling behind, and which work in our research group tries to improve.
At the same time, traditional methods validation in the sense of a simulation study under ideal conditions is insufficient here. Trustworthiness assessments are increasingly likely to be conducted by users of forensic meta-science methods rather than expert developers of these methods. As such, implementations of the methods need to be usable, they need to have UIs that guide users towards making sensible choices and away from non-sensible ones, and they need to have clearly specified interpretations of results and reporting guidelines, etc. We therefore conceptualise validation to be broader, along the following candidate dimensions.
This rubric defines actionable roadmaps for specification, validation, improvement, and the assessment of readiness (rather than being merely aspirational).

text:
Formal specification of method


Logic, math, etc.
Scope of inference
Assumptions
Limitations
Use and failure cases


Implementation


In a free and open-source software library written in an open-source programming language, such as R or Python. In R library or equivalent.
Code as primary output. Treat the implementation as the artefact under review. Open code, unit tests, reproducible fixtures, ;continuous integration.
This often involves additional considerations beyond the abstract method to handle real world use cases. Common considerations include data extraction, which is a whole realm of tasks in itself.
Note that separation of library and tool is important for validation.


Validation against simulated data


e.g., Monte Carlo for stochastic methods, parameter sweep for deterministic methods, etc., to assess whether the method functions as expected over a wide range of known inputs. ADEMP reporting.
Using common performance metrics from research methods, such as sensitivity, specificity, empirical rejection rate (calibration under the null, ability and power to detect issues of what size), bias, coverage, etc.
Robustness to nuisance parameters (e.g., rounded inputs and different rounding or truncation conventions, reporting standards, typos in inputs, number of items).


Validation against human-coded data


To assess whether the method functions as expected over a wide range of realistic inputs. This is useful for surfacing issues to do with extraction/parsing, edge cases, etc.
Consideration of gold vs. reference standards, reporting of inter-rater reliability between human-human, human-tool, or human-ai coders, etc.
This provides information on generalisability, validation within specific domains (e.g., reporting standards may differ between psychology and medicine; pdf formatting may differ between journals or publishers).


Large scale application


Substantive conclusions (e.g., re prevalence, severity etc) from applying the method to a large amount of real world data. Often (initially) using the same data used for validation against human coding, as part of the same process.


Adversarial robustness / gameability.


Once a method is known, can it be evaded (e.g., reporting choices that defeat GRIM)? What vectors of gamability might exist?



Tool


Implementation of the library in a UI tool (eg Shiny app), AI skill, etc. to increase usability/scalability.
Audit trail: does the tool produce an auditable trail of inputs, outputs, versions of method/tool applied, etc.


Reporting standards


Instructions on how to interpret and report results from the method/tool.


Training materials


Materials that train and ideally assess whether users can correctly use and report the method/tool, including its assumptions, limitations, use- and failure-cases etc.


Usability


Evidence that users find the library/tool to be adequately usable; and that misuse cases are assessed, detected and mitigated via human factors research.



Comparison


When multiple implementations of a given or related method are available, head-to-head comparisons are informative. This can be along many of the above dimensions, from validation to usability to training materials, to a general assessment of use-cases.
Versioning, maintenance & deprecation.
Versioning of methods/tools.
Last time of validation. Tools rot (PDF formats change, R deps break). Need for ongoing validation, not one-shot.


Readiness

title: 23  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
23.1 Three layers
A forensic check is usually referred to by a single name: “statcheck flagged this result”, or “this mean fails GRIM”. But every result from a check involves three different things: a method, an implementation of that method, and a tool through which the implementation is used. Each of them can fail, and they fail in different ways. When a check gives an unexpected answer, the first question to ask is which of the three produced it. Treating them as one thing leads to blaming the maths for an error in reading a PDF, or trusting the output of a web page as if it were the maths.
statcheck (Section 10.1.1) is a good example, because “statcheck” can refer to at least three different things, and each can fail in its own way:
The same three layers are present in every check in this book. GRIM is a method, the grim() function in {scrutiny} is an implementation of it, and a web app that calls that function is a tool. The calculators in Chapter 10 are tools that use the implementations in the {recalc} R package.

title: 23  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
What it is
How it can fail




The method
The maths: recalculating a p-value from a test statistic and its degrees of freedom, and the interval that accounts for rounding.
It cannot fail, in the sense that it is provably correct given its inputs and assumptions. But the assumptions may not hold: the test may be one-sided, the p-value may have been corrected, or the degrees of freedom may have been rounded. This can come from the user choosing the wrong settings, or from the article not reporting what was done.


The implementation
The {statcheck} R package: code that applies the method, with particular defaults and decision rules.
Code can contain errors that only arise under particular conditions. Defaults and rules differ between versions, such as whether one-sided tests are searched for, whether p = .000 counts as an error, and whether p = .05 counts as significant. Results from different versions are not always comparable.


The tool
A way of accessing the implementation more easily, such as the web app at statcheck.io, which extracts text from an uploaded file and passes it to the R package.
It may fail to extract the results from the file, or extract them incorrectly. Parsing PDFs is notoriously hard. Different tools that use the same R package can return different results for the same article, because they extract the text differently, such as statcheck.io and statcheck.steveharoz.com.

text:
23.2 What failed?
Keeping the three layers apart makes it clearer what a result means and what to do next. A disagreement between two tools about the same article is usually a disagreement about extraction, not about the maths. A flag that disappears once the right assumption is applied (e.g., one-sided) is a question about the article’s reporting, not about the implementation. And a flag that survives every reasonable assumption, after the numbers have been checked against the original text by hand, is a genuine inconsistency in the method’s own terms.
Each of the problems with statcheck described in Section 10.1.1.4 belongs to one of the layers, and the layer determines what should be done about it:








What happened
Layer
What to do

Check the extracted text against the article


A χ² statistic is read as a statistic named “2” (Schmidt, 2017)

Check the extracted text against the article


p = .000 is counted as an error
Implementation: a default decision rule (pZeroError = TRUE)
Decide whether a reporting convention counts as an error, and set the option accordingly

Implementation: the versions have different options and defaults, such as robust_rounding (Section 10.1.1.1)

Read the article for whether the test was one-sided


A Greenhouse-Geisser corrected p-value is flagged
Method: an assumption does not hold

title: 23  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
23.3 Separation within each layer
Each layer can be divided further, and the same reasoning applies within it: when something fails, it helps to know which part failed.
Within the method, the mathematical identity is distinct from the assumptions needed to apply it and from the decision rules built on top of it. That a two-sided p-value follows from t and its degrees of freedom is an identity. That the test was two-sided, and that the p-value was not corrected afterwards, are assumptions. That a reported p-value is an “inconsistency” if it lies outside the recalculated interval, and a “gross” one if the two fall on opposite sides of α = .05, are decision rules. The identity cannot be wrong, but the assumptions can be, and the decision rules are choices that others might make differently.
Within the implementation, the code that computes the result is distinct from its defaults, from how it handles unusual inputs, and from what it does with inputs that it does not use. Each of these can fail even when the computation is correct. Some examples from the development of {recalc}, the package behind the calculators in Chapter 10:

A default that changed the answer. The subgroup functions require the number of decimal places of every input, and sample sizes were usually given as 0 decimal places. This treats a count as if it had been rounded to the nearest whole number, which lets a reported N that differs from the sum of the subgroups’ ns by a participant or two pass as consistent. Counts are exact, and are now treated as such (Section 10.3.1.1). The maths was right; the default was not.
An edge case that broke the code. The profile likelihood confidence interval for an odds ratio was calculated by fitting a logistic regression and profiling it. When one of the four counts is zero, the model cannot be fitted properly, and the code returned a lower limit of 0 instead of the correct value of about 2. The method, inverting the likelihood ratio test, was fine. Its implementation failed on an input it was not designed for, without any warning.
An input that was accepted but ignored. A function accepted a reported confidence interval for Cohen’s d, but never compared it with the recalculated one. The output therefore never flagged an inconsistent interval, and a reader could easily take the absence of a flag for a pass.

None of these is visible from the maths. They are only found by testing the implementation against the method directly, for example by checking its output against a slow but transparent calculation, or against other implementations, across a wide range of inputs, including unusual ones.
Within the tool, getting the numbers in is distinct from what the tool asks for and infers, and from how it presents the results. Extraction from a PDF is one source of error. What the tool infers is another: the calculators in Chapter 10 take the number of decimal places of each value from the value as it was typed, so a reader who types 4.7 for a reported 4.70 gets a check that allows for more rounding than the article’s numbers had. Presentation is a third: a calculator that says a reported value is “consistent” across a multiverse of analytic choices means that at least one combination of choices could have produced it, not that the authors used that combination.

title: 23  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
23.4 Separation in code
The separation between the layers is worth keeping in code as well as in concepts. The method should be implemented once, in a package function with its own tests, and every tool should call that function rather than reimplementing the maths. Then a fix to the implementation reaches every tool, and the tools cannot quietly disagree with one another about anything except how they get their inputs and display their outputs.
The calculators in this book are built this way. The {recalc} Shiny apps and the webR calculators in Chapter 10 do not reimplement any of the checks. Apart from adding up sample sizes, which needs no R, they call functions in the {recalc} package, and the webR calculators load the package’s code at a fixed version, which they report under their results. The statcheck app in Section 10.1.1.1 does the same with {statcheck}. A tool that copied the formulas into its own code would be a second implementation, and would need testing in its own right.

title: 23  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
23.5 Reporting
In a trustworthiness assessment, report all three layers, so that a reader can tell which of them a result depends on: the method and the assumptions made in applying it, the implementation and its version and settings, and the tool, including how the numbers were entered or extracted. And check every flagged result by hand against the original text before drawing conclusions from it. A check that fails at the tool or implementation layer says nothing about the article.

title: 24  Validating meta-science methods using simulated data ✎ Outline
text:
This chapter will explain, with worked examples and R/tidyverse/purrr code, how to validate implementations of methods against simulated data. It differentiates between exhaustive grid sweeps and probabilistic Monte Carlo simulations.
This form of validation is essential to understanding whether a method works as expected under idea conditions (i.e., assuming no text extraction, parsing, etc issues; just perfect inputs), in terms of false positives, false negatives, coverage, bias, etc.
